Current US national primary ambient air quality standards (NAAQS) for PM2.5, as of 2026-11-16:

- Annual primary PM2.5 standard: 9.0 µg/m³, as an annual arithmetic mean concentration, determined in accordance with 40 CFR Part 50 Appendix N (3-year averaging), met when the annual arithmetic mean is less than or equal to 9.0 µg/m³.
- 24-hour primary PM2.5 standard: 35 µg/m³, as a 98th-percentile 24-hour average concentration, determined in accordance with 40 CFR Part 50 Appendix N (3-year averaging), met when the 98th-percentile 24-hour concentration is less than or equal to 35 µg/m³.

Basis: EPA's February 7, 2024 final reconsideration of the PM NAAQS strengthened the primary annual PM2.5 standard from 12.0 µg/m³ to 9.0 µg/m³ and retained the primary 24-hour PM2.5 standard at 35 µg/m³. EPA's PM NAAQS page states that the primary annual PM2.5 level is set at 9.0 µg/m³ and that the existing 24-hour PM2.5 standard is not being changed. EPA's particle-pollution designations page, last updated October 2, 2026, likewise states that the February 7, 2024 rule strengthened the primary annual PM2.5 NAAQS from 12.0 µg/m³ to 9.0 µg/m³ and retained the 24-hour PM2.5 standard at 35 µg/m³; the 2026 designations activity concerns the 2024 revised annual PM2.5 NAAQS.

Source reconciliation: The retrieved eCFR § 50.18 text displays 12.0 µg/m³ annual and 35 µg/m³ 24-hour with only the 2013 citation [78 FR 3277]. That is the pre-2024 annual level and does not reflect the 2024 reconsideration reflected on EPA's current NAAQS and designations pages. The answer above uses 9.0 µg/m³ as the current primary annual level and 35 µg/m³ as the current primary 24-hour level.

Scope note: These are primary (health-based) standards. Secondary PM2.5 standards are outside the request; in particular, the secondary annual PM2.5 level is not the primary annual level.

# Fall Protection Trigger Height — General Industry (29 CFR 1910, Subpart D)

## 1. Answer

**4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level.**

In general industry (not construction), a US employer must protect each employee on a **walking-working surface with an unprotected side or edge that is 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level** from falling. The trigger is reached at exactly 4 feet — "4 feet or more" — so 4.0 ft is protected-height, not exempt-height.

**Controlling citation:** 29 CFR 1910.28(b)(1)(i). The same 4-foot trigger appears again as the catch-all in 1910.28(b)(15).

## 2. Regulatory text relied on

29 CFR 1910.28(b)(1)(i) — Unprotected sides and edges:

> "General. Except as provided elsewhere in this section, the employer must ensure that each employee on a walking-working surface with an unprotected side or edge that is 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level is protected from falling by one or more of the following: (A) Guardrail systems; (B) Safety net systems; or (C) Personal fall protection systems, such as personal fall arrest, travel restraint, or positioning systems."

29 CFR 1910.28(b)(15) — Walking-working surfaces not otherwise addressed:

> "Except as provided elsewhere in this section or by other subparts of this part, the employer must ensure each employee on a walking-working surface 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level is protected from falling by: (i) Guardrail systems; (ii) Safety net systems; or (iii) Personal fall protection systems, such as personal fall arrest, travel restraint, or positioning systems."

Supporting definitions, 29 CFR 1910.21(b):

> "**Walking-working surface** means any horizontal or vertical surface on or through which an employee walks, works, or gains access to a work area or workplace location."
>
> "**Unprotected sides and edges** mean any side or edge of a walking-working surface (except at entrances and other points of access) where there is no wall, guardrail system, or stair rail system to protect an employee from falling to a lower level."

## 3. When the 4-foot duty is triggered

All three elements must be present:

1. **Employee is on a walking-working surface** — floors, roofs, platforms, runways, ramps, catwalks, walkways, stairway landings, dock/mezzanine surfaces, etc.
2. **That surface has an unprotected side or edge** — i.e., no wall, guardrail system, or stair rail system at that edge. Entrances and other points of access are excluded from "unprotected side or edge."
3. **The edge is 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level.**

The duty attaches on **exposure**, not on duration, task frequency, or intent to work near the edge. There is no "incidental exposure" or "transient task" exception in 1910.28(b)(1). (Task-duration relief exists only in the low-slope-roof provision, §1910.28(b)(13), and in the infeasibility/fall-protection-plan provision, §1910.28(b)(1)(ii).)

Measurement practice: measure from the walking-working surface to the lower level, vertically. Where the surface edge is guarded by a compliant guardrail system or stair rail system per §1910.29, the edge is not "unprotected" and §1910.28(b)(1) does not apply.

## 4. What counts as "protected"

Acceptable under §1910.28(b)(1)(i) — any one or more of:

| Option | Standard for hardware/criteria |
|---|---|
| Guardrail system (passive) | §1910.29(b) — top rail 42 in ± 3 in, midrail, 200 lb load, etc. |
| Safety net system | §1910.29(c) |
| Personal fall protection system: personal fall arrest, travel restraint, or positioning system | §1910.29(d)–(f); PFAS per Subpart I (1910.140) |

Related duties that travel with the trigger: employee training under §1910.30; inspection and maintenance of fall protection systems; falling-object protection under §1910.28(c) where overhead exposure exists; and a written fall protection plan under §1910.29(k) **only** if the employer invokes the infeasibility exception.

**Infeasibility exception — §1910.28(b)(1)(ii):** where the employer can demonstrate that the use of a guardrail, safety net, or personal fall protection system is infeasible or creates a greater hazard, the employer must develop and implement a **fall protection plan** meeting §1910.29(k) that is specific to that location/operation. The exception is employer-demonstrated, not self-declared, and does not waive the 4-foot trigger — it changes the control from a system to a plan.

## 5. Surface-specific variations (do not override the 4-foot default unless listed)

Every row below is quoted or paraphrased from §1910.28(b) as fetched; the 4-foot default governs anything not listed.

| Surface / condition | Trigger | Required protection | Cite |
|---|---|---|---|
| Any walking-working surface with unprotected side/edge | **4 ft (1.2 m)** | Guardrail, safety net, or personal fall protection system | 1910.28(b)(1)(i) |
| Dangerous equipment — employee *less than* 4 ft above it | any height below 4 ft | Guardrail system or travel restraint system, unless equipment is covered/guarded to eliminate the hazard | 1910.28(b)(6)(i) |
| Dangerous equipment — employee 4 ft or more above it | **4 ft (1.2 m)** | Guardrail, safety net, travel restraint, or PFAS | 1910.28(b)(6)(ii) |
| Openings (inside bottom edge < 39 in above surface, outside bottom edge ≥ 4 ft above lower level) | **4 ft (1.2 m)** | Guardrail, safety net, travel restraint, or PFAS | 1910.28(b)(7) |
| Stairway landing with unprotected side or edge | **4 ft (1.2 m)** | Guardrail or stair rail system | 1910.28(b)(11)(i) |
| Rope descent system | **4 ft (1.2 m)** | Personal fall arrest system | 1910.28(b)(12)(ii) |
| Slaughtering facility platform, unprotected working side | **4 ft (1.2 m)** | Guardrail or travel restraint (infeasibility pathway available with training) | 1910.28(b)(14) |
| Walking-working surfaces not otherwise addressed | **4 ft (1.2 m)** | Guardrail, safety net, or personal fall protection system | 1910.28(b)(15) |
| Low-slope roofs | Keyed to **distance from edge**, not height: < 6 ft from edge — full system; 6 to < 15 ft — full system, designated area allowed for infrequent/temporary work; ≥ 15 ft — system or designated area, and no fall protection required if work is both infrequent and temporary, plus a work rule barring employees within 15 ft of the edge without protection | Guardrail, safety net, travel restraint, PFAS, or designated area as applicable | 1910.28(b)(13) |
| Scaffolds | Referred out of Part 1910: employees on a scaffold are protected per **29 CFR 1926 Subpart L**, whose fall-protection trigger is 10 ft above a lower level (1926.451(g)(1)) | Per 1926 Subpart L | 1910.28(b)(12)(i) |
| Fixed ladders extending more than 24 ft above a lower level | Separate regime (ladder safety system / PFAS, with the 2036 phase-out of cages and wells) | Ladder safety system or PFAS | 1910.28(b)(9) |

## 6. Adjacent traps (stated so they are not mistaken for the answer)

- **Construction is different.** 29 CFR 1926.501(b)(1) sets the construction trigger at **6 feet**. That is *not* the general-industry answer and must not be applied to §1910-covered general-industry walking-working surfaces. Scaffolding is the one place general industry explicitly imports a Part 1926 rule (see table above).
- **Shipyard, marine terminals, longshoring, and agricultural operations** are covered by their own Parts (1915, 1917, 1918, 1928) and are outside this answer's scope.
- **State-plan states** must be at least as effective as the federal standard but may be stricter or may use different trigger heights for some surfaces; the applicable state plan governs in those jurisdictions. Verify jurisdiction before relying on the federal 4-foot figure.
- **Pre-2017 general industry rules** also used a 4-foot trigger for open-sided floors and platforms (former §1910.23(c)), so the 4-foot answer is stable across the 2016/2017 Subpart D rewrite; the current citation is §1910.28.

## 7. Application procedure (how an employer closes this out)

1. **Inventory** every walking-working surface employees use: floors, mezzanines, platforms, catwalks, runways, ramps, roofs, stairway landings, dock edges, pits, roof hatches.
2. **Measure** each unprotected edge vertically to the lower level. Record the dimension and the measurement datum.
3. **Classify** each edge:
   - Guarded by a compliant wall/guardrail/stair rail per §1910.29 → no §1910.28(b)(1) duty; maintain and inspect it.
   - **≥ 4 ft** and unprotected → duty attaches; select guardrail, safety net, or personal fall protection system.
   - < 4 ft and unprotected → §1910.28(b)(1) does not apply, but check §1910.28(b)(6) (dangerous equipment — duty can attach below 4 ft) and §1910.28(b)(3)/(7) (holes and openings) before closing the item.
   - Low-slope roof → apply the edge-distance scheme in §1910.28(b)(13) instead of a height-only test.
   - Scaffold or fixed ladder → apply §1926 Subpart L or §1910.28(b)(9) respectively.
4. **Engineer the control**: specify the system, cite the §1910.29 criteria it must meet, and identify anchorages (2x intended load / 5,000 lb per employee for PFAS, per §1910.140).
5. **Train** affected employees under §1910.30 before exposure, and document it.
6. **If invoking infeasibility**, write the §1910.29(k) fall protection plan, document why a system is infeasible or creates a greater hazard, and restrict access to trained authorized employees.
7. **Re-verify** whenever a surface, edge condition, or task changes.

## 8. One-line citation block

> 29 CFR 1910.28(b)(1)(i): each employee on a walking-working surface with an unprotected side or edge **4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level** must be protected by a guardrail system, safety net system, or personal fall protection system. Catch-all at 29 CFR 1910.28(b)(15) restates the same 4-foot (1.2 m) trigger.

# Reserve fuel for a helicopter beginning a VFR flight in the US

## 1. Answer

**20 minutes.** A helicopter (rotorcraft) may not begin a VFR flight in the US unless, considering wind and forecast weather conditions, it carries enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing **and then fly for at least 20 minutes at normal cruising speed**.

The reserve is expressed as **time**, not distance and not a fixed volume. The volume of fuel that satisfies it depends on the individual helicopter's cruise fuel burn: reserve volume = (20/60) x cruise fuel flow.

This is the legal minimum at the moment the flight begins. It is a single number for both day and night VFR — there is no night increase for rotorcraft.

## 2. Controlling regulatory text

14 CFR §91.151 (Fuel requirements for flight in VFR conditions), verbatim:

> (a) No person may begin a flight in an airplane under VFR conditions unless (considering wind and forecast weather conditions) there is enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising speed—
> (1) During the day, to fly after that for at least 30 minutes; or
> (2) At night, to fly after that for at least 45 minutes.
>
> (b) No person may begin a flight in a rotorcraft under VFR conditions unless (considering wind and forecast weather conditions) there is enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising speed, to fly after that for at least 20 minutes.

For a commercial helicopter operator, 14 CFR §135.209(b) is materially identical:

> (b) No person may begin a flight operation in a helicopter under VFR unless, considering wind and forecast weather conditions, it has enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising fuel consumption, to fly after that for at least 20 minutes.

So the answer is **20 minutes** whether the flight is flown under Part 91 general operating rules or under Part 135. The number does not change; only the citation and the enforcement mechanism change.

## 3. Applicability matrix

| Operation | Rule | Reserve beyond first point of intended landing |
|---|---|---|
| Helicopter, VFR, day, Part 91 | §91.151(b) | **20 minutes** |
| Helicopter, VFR, night, Part 91 | §91.151(b) | **20 minutes** (no night increase) |
| Helicopter, VFR, day, Part 135 | §135.209(b) | **20 minutes** |
| Helicopter, VFR, night, Part 135 | §135.209(b) | **20 minutes** (no night increase) |
| Gyroplane / other rotorcraft, VFR, Part 91 | §91.151(b) | **20 minutes** (§91.151(b) says "rotorcraft," not "helicopter") |
| Airplane, VFR, day (for contrast only — NOT applicable to helicopters) | §91.151(a)(1) | 30 minutes |
| Airplane, VFR, night (for contrast only — NOT applicable to helicopters) | §91.151(a)(2) | 45 minutes |

Key structural point: §91.151 splits by **airplane vs. rotorcraft**, not by day vs. night. The 30/45-minute day/night ladder belongs entirely to paragraph (a) and has no rotorcraft counterpart. Any plan that applies 30 or 45 minutes to a helicopter over-complies; any plan that applies less than 20 minutes is unlawful.

## 4. Converting the 20-minute reserve into fuel quantity

Procedure:

1. Determine the helicopter's **normal cruising speed** and the **fuel flow at that speed** from the POH/AFM (typically the cruise performance table at the planned cruise altitude and temperature, leaned per the POH). Use **usable** fuel.
2. Compute reserve volume: `Reserve = (20 / 60) x cruise fuel flow`.
3. Compute trip fuel: fuel to reach the first point of intended landing, adjusted for forecast wind and temperature.
4. Minimum fuel at start of flight: `Trip fuel + Reserve` (plus any taxi/run-up/departure fuel the operator chooses to plan, which is separate from the regulatory reserve).
5. Convert to a fuel-gauge/time cross-check: the reserve must be readable as at least 20 minutes of cruise endurance on the fuel totalizer/time remaining at brake release.

Worked example (illustrative numbers, not type data): cruise 120 KTAS, cruise fuel flow 30 gal/hr.

- Reserve = (20/60) x 30 = **10.0 gal**
- Check: 10.0 gal / 30 gal/hr = 0.3333 hr = **20.0 min** ✓
- Equivalent still-air distance at 120 kt: 20 min = 40 nm (illustration of what the reserve buys, not a regulatory distance requirement)

Second illustration at a lighter burn: 15 gal/hr cruise -> reserve = (20/60) x 15 = **5.0 gal** (check: 5.0/15 = 0.3333 hr = 20.0 min ✓).

Because the rule is time-based, the reserve volume scales linearly with the aircraft's cruise burn. There is no single gallon figure that is correct across types; quoting one is an error.

## 5. Planning rules and interpretation notes

- **Measured at departure.** The rule says "may begin a flight ... unless there is enough fuel." Compliance is judged at the start of the flight. The 20 minutes is a minimum fuel state at departure, not a target to be consumed en route.
- **"Normal cruising speed" is the yardstick.** The reserve is 20 minutes of endurance at the speed the aircraft will normally cruise, not at best-range or max-endurance speed. Do not stretch the reserve by assuming a slower speed than the flight will actually be flown.
- **Wind and forecast weather are considered for the leg, not to shrink the reserve.** The regulation's wind/forecast qualifier applies to the fuel needed to reach the first point of intended landing; the 20 minutes is added after that.
- **First point of intended landing** means the first planned landing of the flight, not an alternate and not a later stop. Fuel to subsequent legs is a separate planning matter and is not part of the §91.151(b) reserve.
- **Night VFR:** no additional reserve is required by §91.151(b). Night VFR does change equipment and, for airplanes only, other rules — do not import the airplane 45-minute night figure.
- **Company/operator policy, OpSpecs, and POH limitations may exceed 20 minutes** and frequently do (offshore, overwater, remote-area operations). The regulatory minimum is a floor, not a recommendation.
- **Enforcement reality:** the reserve is unusable fuel for planning purposes. Plan the flight so the 20 minutes is intact at the first landing, not merely present at takeoff on paper.

## 6. Explicit scope exclusions

- **IFR flight:** governed by different sections (§91.167 for Part 91, §135.223 for Part 135). Out of scope; no IFR figure is stated here because it is a different question and would not be a VFR reserve.
- **Overwater / offshore operations:** additional fuel or equipment rules and operator policy may apply.
- **Non-US operations:** other authorities (EASA, UK CAA, etc.) set different helicopter VFR reserves; this answer is US-only.
- **Company fuel policy:** not a regulatory minimum and not addressed.

## 7. One-line restatement

A helicopter beginning a VFR flight in the US must carry fuel to the first point of intended landing plus **20 minutes at normal cruising speed** (14 CFR §91.151(b); equivalently §135.209(b) for Part 135), day or night, with no alternate and no distance-based component.

# Deprecation of TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 — answer with primary-source grounding

## 1. Direct answers

| Ask | Answer |
|---|---|
| 1. Which RFC deprecated TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1? | **RFC 8996**, *Deprecating TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1* (BCP 195) |
| 2. What status did it give the RFCs that defined them? | **Historic** — applied to both defining RFCs: RFC 2246 (TLS 1.0) and RFC 4346 (TLS 1.1) |

## 2. The sentence that answers both asks

From the RFC 8996 abstract (identical text at https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8996.html, in sections 1–3, in https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8996.xml, and at https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc8996/):

> "This document formally deprecates Transport Layer Security (TLS) versions 1.0 (RFC 2246) and 1.1 (RFC 4346). Accordingly, those documents have been moved to Historic status."

That single passage supplies both values: the deprecating document is RFC 8996; the status conferred on RFC 2246 and RFC 4346 is Historic.

## 3. Disposition table (what RFC 8996 did, document by document)

| Document | What it defined | Action taken by RFC 8996 | Status after |
|---|---|---|---|
| RFC 2246 | TLS 1.0 | Formally deprecated; moved to Historic | **Historic** |
| RFC 4346 | TLS 1.1 | Formally deprecated; moved to Historic | **Historic** |
| RFC 4347 | DTLS 1.0 | Deprecated ("This document also deprecates Datagram TLS (DTLS) version 1.0 (RFC 4347)") | Not stated in the fetched passages — see §6 |
| RFC 6347 | DTLS 1.2 | Not deprecated; updated (negotiation of DTLS 1.0 now forbidden) | Unchanged |
| RFC 5469 | DES/IDEA cipher suites | Moved to Historic (collateral: "since the only versions of TLS for which their usage is defined are now Historic, [RFC5469] has been moved to Historic as well") | Historic |
| RFC 7507 | TLS Fallback SCSV | Marked **Obsolete** (superseded by the TLS 1.3 ServerHello.Random mechanism) | Obsolete |
| RFC 7525 | TLS best-practice BCP | Updated (RFC 8996 becomes part of BCP 195) | Updated |

Rows 3–7 are context only. **The answer to ask 2 is the top two rows: Historic, for both RFC 2246 and RFC 4346.**

## 4. Terminology note — "deprecated" vs. "Historic" vs. "Obsolete"

These are three distinct things in IETF usage, and the question deliberately spans two of them:

- **Deprecate** is the *act* RFC 8996 performs ("This document formally deprecates ...").
- **Historic** is the *RFC status label* that results, and it is the status the question asks about. In the IETF status taxonomy, Historic is the designation for a specification that has been superseded or is no longer recommended for new use; RFC 8996 states it directly: "those documents have been moved to Historic status."
- **Obsolete** is a different label, used in the same RFC for a different document (RFC 7507). Do not conflate it with the answer: RFC 8996 does **not** say RFC 2246 or RFC 4346 were made Obsolete. Its own wording is "moved to Historic status."

So the precise phrasing of the answer is: RFC 8996 *deprecated* TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 and moved their defining RFCs (RFC 2246, RFC 4346) to *Historic* status.

## 5. Supporting normative content (why the Historic move is operative, not cosmetic)

RFC 8996 does not merely re-label; it forbids the protocols:

- TLS 1.0 — "TLS 1.0 MUST NOT be used. Negotiation of TLS 1.0 from any version of TLS MUST NOT be permitted." Clients MUST NOT send `ClientHello.client_version = {03,01}`; servers MUST NOT send `ServerHello.server_version = {03,01}`; a receiver of such a Hello MUST respond with a `protocol_version` alert and close the connection. Servers MUST still accept any `{03,XX}` record-layer version (including `{03,00}`) in ClientHello for interoperability, but MUST NOT negotiate TLS 1.0.
- TLS 1.1 — "TLS 1.1 MUST NOT be used. Negotiation of TLS 1.1 from any version of TLS MUST NOT be permitted." Same wire-level prohibition with `{03,02}`.

## 6. Scope, caveats, and what is deliberately not asserted

- **Both defining RFCs, one status.** RFC 2246 (TLS 1.0) and RFC 4346 (TLS 1.1) both receive Historic; there is no per-version difference to report.
- **DTLS 1.0 (RFC 4347).** RFC 8996 says it "deprecates" DTLS 1.0, but the fetched passages do not contain a sentence moving RFC 4347 to Historic. I therefore do not assert a status for RFC 4347. It is outside the question anyway, which asks only about the RFCs that defined TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1.
- **Publication metadata.** The fetched text grounds the title, the BCP 195 membership, and the fact that it updates RFC 7525 ("This memo documents an Internet Best Current Practice"). The publication date (commonly cited as March 2021) and the exact header fields (e.g. the Obsoletes/Updates lists) were **not** present in the fetched excerpts and are not relied on here; verify against https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc8996/ if a citation with date is required.
- **Later errata/updates.** No later document altering the Historic status of RFC 2246 or RFC 4346 appears in the grounding; the answer reflects RFC 8996 as published.
- **Non-IETF deprecations.** Industry and government profile mandates (e.g. PCI, NIST, browser removal of TLS 1.0/1.1) are acknowledged in the RFC's own rationale but are not the formal deprecation asked about; RFC 8996 is.

## 7. Copy-ready citation

> RFC 8996, *Deprecating TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1*, BCP 195 (Internet Best Current Practice), IETF. Abstract: "This document formally deprecates Transport Layer Security (TLS) versions 1.0 (RFC 2246) and 1.1 (RFC 4346). Accordingly, those documents have been moved to Historic status." https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8996.html

The US Social Security contribution and benefit base (the OASDI taxable maximum — the maximum amount of an individual's wages, and of net earnings from self-employment, subject to the Social Security payroll tax) for calendar year 2026 is:

  $184,500

This is the officially published figure, not an estimate or projection. It applies to earnings in 2026, per person, on a combined wage basis across all jobs (not per job and not per household).

1. CORROBORATION (three independent SSA statements agree)

  a) SSA Office of the Chief Actuary, "Contribution and Benefit Base" table (ssa.gov/OACT/cola/cbb.html): the annual series reads ... 2024 $168,600; 2025 $176,100; 2026 $184,500; 2027 $192,300. The 2026 entry is $184,500.

  b) SSA Publication No. 05-10024, "What's inside / Your Social Security taxes" (2026 edition): "You pay Social Security taxes based on your earnings, up to a certain amount. In 2026 that amount is $184,500." The same publication gives the rates applied to that base: 6.2% employee + 6.2% employer; 12.4% self-employed.

  c) SSA Office of the Chief Actuary, "Automatic Determinations — Contribution & Benefit Base" (ssa.gov/OACT/cola/cbbdet.html): in setting the 2027 base, SSA states the 2027 amount of $192,300 "exceeds the base for 2026," which it identifies as $184,500 (the statutory no-decrease floor).

No 2026 legislation altering the taxable maximum appears in the sourced material; the figure is the product of the ordinary statutory wage-index adjustment.

2. DERIVATION UNDER THE STATUTORY FORMULA (independent arithmetic check)

  Formula (Social Security Act, as described on SSA's determination page): for year Y after 1994,
      base(Y) = $60,600 x [ AWI(Y-2) / AWI(1992) ], rounded to the nearest multiple of $300;
      never reduced below the prior year's base.
  Inputs: 1994 base = $60,600; AWI(1992) = $22,935.42; AWI(2024) = $69,846.49 (as reported in SSA's 2026 determination/COLA materials).

  Computation:
      $60,600 x ($69,846.49 / $22,935.42) = $60,600 x 3.045355... = $184,548.5
      Nearest multiple of $300: $184,548.5 sits $48.50 above $184,500 and $251.50 below $184,800
      => $184,500
      $184,500 > $176,100 (2025 base), so the no-decrease rule is not triggered.

  Robustness: the result is $184,500 for any 2024 AWI in roughly $69,782 to $69,887 (the band within which the computed amount stays inside [$184,350, $184,650)). The published $184,500 is therefore not sensitive to rounding of the AWI input.

3. FIGURES THAT FOLLOW FROM THE BASE (for payroll-system and payroll-tax use)

  - Employee OASDI: 6.2% x $184,500 = $11,439.00 maximum withholding for 2026.
  - Employer OASDI: 6.2% x $184,500 = $11,439.00 per employee for 2026.
  - Combined OASDI on wages at or above the base: $22,878.00.
  - Self-employed OASDI (SECA): 12.4% x $184,500 = $22,878.00, computed on net earnings from self-employment up to the base (with the employer-equivalent deduction applied to net earnings before the 12.4% is figured, per normal Schedule SE mechanics).
  - Medicare (HI): NO earnings cap for 2026 (the HI taxable maximum was eliminated after 1993); 1.45% each on all wages, 2.9% on all self-employment earnings, plus the 0.9% Additional Medicare Tax above $200,000 single / $250,000 married-filing-jointly / $125,000 married-filing-separately thresholds. Do not apply $184,500 to Medicare.
  - The same $184,500 is also the maximum earnings creditable toward a 2026 benefit computation (the base serves both the tax cap and the benefit-credit cap).
  - 2026 earnings credit: 1 credit per $1,890, maximum 4 credits ($7,560) — well below the base; included only to prevent conflation with the base.

4. CONVENTIONS AND SCOPE

  - Currency/rounding: US dollars, whole dollars; the base is by statute a multiple of $300.
  - Year: calendar year 2026 (wages paid Jan 1 - Dec 31, 2026; self-employment income for tax year 2026).
  - Program scope: Old-Age, Survivors, and Disability Insurance (OASDI) only — this is the standard meaning of "contribution and benefit base."
  - Not the 2025 figure ($176,100) and not the already-determined 2027 figure ($192,300).
  - If a figure is needed for a plan year or fiscal year that straddles calendar years, use $184,500 for the 2026 portion and $192,300 for the 2027 portion.

question: M12
answer:
ANSWER

The 2026 limit on an employee's elective deferrals to a 401(k) plan, before any catch-up contribution, is $24,500.

This is the IRC § 402(g)(1) elective deferral limit for calendar year 2026. It is a published, final figure — not a projection — announced by the IRS on November 13, 2025 in News Release IR-2025-111 and set out in Notice 2025-67 ("2026 Amounts Relating to Retirement Plans and IRAs, as Adjusted for Changes in Cost-of-Living"). It is an increase from $23,500 in 2025.

AUTHORITY AND EXACT LANGUAGE

- Notice 2025-67: "The limitation under section 402(g)(1) on the exclusion for elective deferrals described in section 402(g)(3), which includes elective deferrals made to the Thrift Savings Plan, is increased from $23,500 to $24,500."
- IR-2025-111: "The annual contribution limit for employees who participate in 401(k), 403(b), governmental 457 plans, and the federal government's Thrift Savings Plan is increased to $24,500, up from $23,500 for 2025."
- IRS Retirement Topics – 401(k) and Profit-Sharing Plan Contribution Limits: "The limit on employee elective deferrals (for traditional and safe harbor plans) is: $24,500 in 2026, subject to cost-of-living adjustments."
- Publication 560: "In 2026, the $350,000 limit increases to $360,000, and the $23,500 limit increases to $24,500."

SCOPE — WHAT THE $24,500 DOES AND DOES NOT COVER

Counts toward the $24,500:
- Pre-tax (traditional) elective deferrals.
- Designated Roth elective deferrals. Roth 401(k) deferrals share the same $24,500 bucket; they do not get a separate limit.
- Deferrals to all 401(k) plans of all employers in which the individual participates during the year. The limit is per individual, per calendar year, aggregated — not per employer and not per plan.
- The same $24,500 figure applies to 403(b) plans, governmental 457(b) plans, and the Thrift Savings Plan; a person participating in more than one of these must aggregate across them as well (with the standard 457(b)/402(g) coordination rules applied by payroll).

Does NOT count toward the $24,500:
- Catch-up contributions (age 50+ and the age 60–63 enhanced tier). These are additional and are expressly excluded from this question.
- Employer matching contributions and employer nonelective/profit-sharing contributions.
- Forfeiture allocations.
- Rollover contributions.
- After-tax (non-Roth) employee contributions, where the plan permits them — these are tested against the § 415(c) annual additions limit, not § 402(g).

ADJACENT 2026 FIGURES — FOR PAYROLL SETUP ONLY (do not confuse with the answer)

- Age 50+ catch-up (standard): $8,000 (up from $7,500). Maximum employee deferral for a participant age 50+ in 2026: $24,500 + $8,000 = $32,500.
- Age 60–63 enhanced catch-up (SECURE 2.0 § 109): $11,250 for 2026 (unchanged). Maximum employee deferral for a participant attaining age 60, 61, 62, or 63 in 2026: $24,500 + $11,250 = $35,750.
- § 415(c) total annual additions: lesser of 100% of compensation or $72,000. Including catch-up: $80,000, or up to $83,250 for participants age 60–63.
- § 401(a)(17) compensation cap: $360,000.
- SIMPLE 401(k) elective deferral limit: $17,000 (a different plan type — a SIMPLE 401(k) is not subject to the $24,500 figure).
- Starter 401(k) / safe harbor deferral-only 403(b) limit: $6,000 (a different plan type).

HR / PAYROLL ADMINISTRATION NOTES

1. Per-paycheck conversion. For a salaried employee paid semi-monthly (24 pay periods), the level per-paycheck deferral that exactly reaches $24,500 is $24,500 / 24 = $1,020.83. For biweekly (26 periods), $24,500 / 26 = $942.31. For monthly (12 periods), $24,500 / 12 = $2,041.67. Round down at the payroll system level and let the final period true up, so the system does not overshoot the limit.
2. Mid-year hires and mid-year limit changes. Prorate only if the plan document so provides; the statutory limit is a full-year dollar cap, not a percentage. A mid-year hire may defer up to the full $24,500 for the year unless the plan imposes a lower cap.
3. Plans may be stricter. A plan document may impose a lower deferral cap, and nondiscrimination testing (ADP) may force a lower cap on highly compensated employees mid-year. The $24,500 is a ceiling, not an entitlement.
4. Multiple employers / job changes. Because the limit is per person, an employee who changes jobs mid-year must tell the new employer's payroll what has already been deferred. Absent that, the employee — not the plan — bears the excess-deferral correction: excess amounts are includible in income in the year deferred and must be distributed (with allocable earnings) by April 15 of the following year to avoid double taxation. Payroll should capture year-to-date deferrals at onboarding.
5. Roth coordination. Do not create a separate $24,500 bucket for Roth. Pre-tax plus Roth deferrals combined must be monitored against the single $24,500 cap.
6. Excess deferral correction. If the cap is breached, the plan's correction is a distribution of the excess plus earnings by the April 15 deadline; the § 402(g) excess is taxable in the year of deferral even if distributed timely. Report on Form 1099-R.
7. Documentation. Keep the IRS announcement (Notice 2025-67 / IR-2025-111) in the plan's administrative file as the authority for the 2026 payroll limit, and update the plan's deferral election forms and payroll system limits effective the first pay period beginning on or after January 1, 2026.

ONE-LINE ANSWER FOR THE RECORD

2026 § 402(g) elective deferral limit, excluding catch-up: $24,500.

answer:
BASICMED AIRCRAFT LIMITS — CURRENT (POST-NOVEMBER 2024) LAW

1. THE THREE ANSWERS

| # | Limit | Current value | Governing provision |
|---|-------|---------------|---------------------|
| 1 | Maximum certificated takeoff weight | 12,500 lb (5,670 kg) | 14 CFR 61.113(i)(1), as amended per P.L. 118-63 § 252 |
| 2 | Occupants the aircraft may be authorized to carry | 7 occupants (including required flightcrew) | 14 CFR 61.113(i)(1) |
| 3 | Passengers on board | 6 passengers | 14 CFR 61.113(i)(1) |

Exception carried by the statute and the FAA release: the 12,500 lb weight increase does NOT extend to transport-category helicopters; those remain subject to the 6,000 lb maximum takeoff weight.

2. WHY THESE VALUES AND NOT 6,000 lb / 6 / 5 — SOURCE HIERARCHY AND TIMELINE

The grounding contains two generations of the rule. They must not be blended.

SUPERSEDED (pre-amendment) figures: 6,000 lb maximum takeoff weight, 6 occupants authorized, 5 passengers on board. These appear in:
- 14 CFR 61.113(i)(1) as printed in the 2024 annual CFR volume (quoted: "authorized to carry not more than 6 occupants, has a maximum takeoff weight of not more than 6,000 pounds, and is operated with no more than five passengers on board");
- AC 68-1A, dated 5/3/17, § 3.2 ("no more than five passengers … 6,000 lbs … no more than 6 occupants") and § 5.2.1;
- FAA Form 8700-2 (CMEC), which still recites "not more than 6 occupants … not more than 6,000 pounds";
- the FAA Safety Briefing "BasicMed One Departure" graphic (1 MAY 17).

CURRENT figures: 12,500 lb, 7 occupants, 6 passengers. Authority:
- FAA newsroom, Friday, November 15, 2024, "FAA Updates BasicMed Program": "The FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024 required the FAA to expand BasicMed to: Increase the number of allowable passengers to six from five, and the number of occupants to seven from six. Increase the maximum aircraft takeoff weight to 12,500 lbs. from 6,000 lbs., excluding transport category helicopters."
- FAA BasicMed program page, "Aircraft Requirements": "Any aircraft authorized under federal law to carry not more than 7 occupants; Has a maximum certificated takeoff weight of not more than 12,500 pounds." "Operating Requirements: Carries not more than six passengers."

Resolution rule applied: the CFR annual edition is a snapshot printed before the November 2024 amendment, and AC 68-1A / Form 8700-2 / the 2017 briefing graphic are pre-amendment guidance artifacts. The FAA's program page and the dated rulemaking announcement reflect the rule now in force. Where a printed artifact and the operative rule conflict, the operative rule controls. Any flight conducted before the amendment's effective date was lawfully flown to the old figures; that does not make them current.

Documentation-lag warning for reviewers: a pilot or mechanic who checks only AC 68-1A or the printed CMEC will still see 6,000/6/5. Those documents lag the rule. The verification step in §7 below tells you how to confirm the live text.

3. WHAT EACH LIMIT ACTUALLY MEASURES

3.1 Maximum takeoff weight (ask 1) — 12,500 lb.
This is the aircraft's maximum certificated takeoff weight, i.e., the MTOW established by its design approval (type certificate, supplemental type certificate, or amended TC) and stated in the AFM/POH and Type Certificate Data Sheet. It is not the actual takeoff weight on a given flight; an aircraft certificated at 12,500 lb qualifies even when departing at 9,800 lb, and an aircraft certificated at 13,000 lb does not qualify even if it happens to depart light. Where an aircraft has been altered to a lower certificated MTOW by STC/ATC (e.g., a 12,800 lb type modified to 12,500 lb or below), the altered certificated weight governs, and the STC/ATC paperwork must be on the aircraft.

3.2 Occupants the aircraft may be authorized to carry (ask 2) — 7.
"Authorized to carry" is a property of the aircraft's design approval, not of who shows up. It is the maximum occupant count the TC/STC/ATC (or, for experimental/amateur-built, the operating limitations issued under § 91.319) authorizes — and it includes required flightcrew. An aircraft type-certificated for 8 occupants does not become compliant by flying with 7 aboard; it is ineligible. Conversely, an aircraft originally certificated above 7 occupants that has been altered by STC/ATC to 7 or fewer is eligible (this is the mechanism AC 68-1A § 5.1.2 describes, using the old six-occupant number; the logic carries over unchanged to seven).

3.3 Passengers on board (ask 3) — 6.
This is a per-flight count of persons carried other than the pilot in command and other required flightcrew. It is the only one of the three limits that is about the flight rather than the aircraft.

3.4 How the three interact — worked cases
- One-pilot aircraft, 7 occupants authorized, 7 seats: PIC + 6 passengers = 7 occupants, 6 passengers. Both limits exactly met. Legal.
- Same aircraft with 7 passengers: 8 occupants, 7 passengers. Fails both. Illegal.
- Aircraft type-certificated for two required pilots, 7 occupants authorized: 2 required flightcrew + 5 passengers = 7 occupants, 5 passengers. Legal — and note the passenger count (5) is below the cap of 6; the occupant cap is the binding constraint here.
- Aircraft type-certificated for two required pilots and 8 occupants: ineligible regardless of how many people board.
- An occupant who is a non-required pilot (e.g., a safety pilot or a rated friend riding along) counts as a passenger for the 6-passenger limit unless the aircraft's type certificate requires that crewmember.

4. SPECIAL AIRCRAFT CATEGORIES

- Transport-category helicopters: the 12,500 lb increase does not apply; 6,000 lb maximum certificated takeoff weight remains the ceiling for these under BasicMed (FAA release, 15 Nov 2024). The 7-occupant / 6-passenger limits are unaffected by that carve-out.
- Experimental/amateur-built: occupant limits come from the § 91.319 operating limitations; § 91.319(j) separately bars carrying more than the BasicMed occupant ceiling under BasicMed. Confirm the current § 91.319(j) text against the eCFR, as it was conformed to the amended occupant count.
- Light-sport, gliders, balloons, rotorcraft: no separate weight relief; the same 12,500 lb / 7 occupant / 6 passenger tests apply, subject to each aircraft's own design approval or operating limitations.
- Aircraft with no certificated MTOW (some experimental/exhibition): use the maximum weight established in the operating limitations; if no such weight is established, treat the aircraft as outside BasicMed until the FAA guidance for that configuration is confirmed.

5. ADJACENT BASICMED OPERATING LIMITS (not asked, stated for completeness)

Under 14 CFR 61.113(i)(2) and AC 68-1A § 3.2, the flight itself must also be:
- within the United States;
- at or below 18,000 ft MSL;
- at an indicated airspeed of 250 knots or less;
- not for compensation or hire;
- day or night, VFR or IFR is permitted;
- no flight during a medical deficiency (14 CFR 61.53).
Pilot-side eligibility: valid U.S. driver's license; have held an FAA medical certificate at any point after 14 July 2006 (most recent not denied/revoked/suspended, special issuance not withdrawn); CMEC completed with a state-licensed physician (FAA Form 8700-2); BasicMed online education course completed; documents retained (digital copies acceptable).

6. SCOPE AND ASSUMPTIONS

- Jurisdiction: United States, 14 CFR Part 68 / § 61.113(i), FAA guidance in force after the November 2024 update. No foreign authority, exemption, deviation, or equivalent (e.g., Canada's Cat 4, UK PMD) is addressed.
- The pilot satisfies all BasicMed eligibility conditions, so the aircraft and flight limits are the operative constraints.
- These are regulatory eligibility limits on the aircraft and flight, not operator, insurer, club, or rental-agreement restrictions, which may be stricter and are not reflected here.
- The limits apply to the whole flight, takeoff to touchdown, and must be verified per aircraft, per flight.

7. HOW TO VERIFY BEFORE FLYING (procedure)

Step 1 — Check the live rule text: eCFR, 14 CFR 61.113(i)(1), current date. Expect "not more than 7 occupants … maximum takeoff weight of not more than 12,500 pounds … no more than six passengers." If the text still shows 6/6,000/5, the edition being viewed is stale — check the amendment date on the section.
Step 2 — Check FAA BasicMed program page (faa.gov/licenses_certificates/airmen_certification/basic_med), "Aircraft Requirements" and "Operating Requirements" blocks, which state 7 occupants / 12,500 lb / 6 passengers.
Step 3 — Check for the current edition of AC 68-1 (the copy in hand is AC 68-1A, 5/3/17, still carrying the old numbers; a later revision, if issued, supersedes it).
Step 4 — For the specific aircraft: pull the TCDS and the AFM/POH limitation section to read certificated MTOW and certificated maximum occupant count; for experimental aircraft read the § 91.319 operating limitations. Confirm any STC/ATC that changes either value is installed and documented.
Step 5 — Compute the planned load: occupants = required crew + all others; passengers = all aboard except the PIC and required crew. Both must be within 7 and 6 respectively, and planned takeoff weight must be at or below the certificated MTOW (which itself must be at or below 12,500 lb, or 6,000 lb for a transport-category helicopter).

8. CITATIONS

- 14 CFR 61.113(i)(1) — occupant, weight and passenger conditions (text as amended; the 2024 annual CFR volume print still shows the pre-amendment 6 / 6,000 lb / 5 figures).
- 14 CFR 61.113(i)(2) — altitude, speed, and geographic limits.
- 14 CFR 91.319(j) — experimental aircraft occupant limit under BasicMed.
- 14 CFR Part 68; FAA Form 8700-2 (CMEC) — pilot eligibility and examination checklist (form still recites the pre-amendment 6 occupant / 6,000 lb figures; it is a medical checklist, not the operative aircraft limit).
- FAA Advisory Circular AC 68-1A, 5/3/17, § 3.2, § 5.1.2, § 5.2.1 — BasicMed privileges and the design-approval (TC/STC/ATC) test for occupant count and MTOW; § 5.1.2 is the authority for the point that an aircraft altered to a lower certificated occupant count or MTOW qualifies.
- FAA, "FAA Updates BasicMed Program," 15 November 2024 — announces the expansion to 6 passengers, 7 occupants, 12,500 lb, excluding transport-category helicopters.
- FAA BasicMed program page — "Any aircraft authorized under federal law to carry not more than 7 occupants; Has a maximum certificated takeoff weight of not more than 12,500 pounds … Carries not more than six passengers."
- FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024, P.L. 118-63, § 252 — statutory direction for the expansion.

question: M3
answer:
# Hours of service — driver of a passenger-carrying CMV (motorcoach), US federal

## Scope and authority
49 CFR Part 395, specifically **§ 395.5, "Maximum driving time for passenger-carrying vehicles,"** subject to the exceptions and exemptions in § 395.1. A motorcoach is a *passenger-carrying* commercial motor vehicle, so § 395.5 governs — not § 395.3 (property-carrying). The text below was verified against three sources that agree verbatim: eCFR § 395.5, the 2025 edition of 49 CFR vol. 5 (govinfo), and FMCSA's "Hours of Service for Motor Carriers of Passengers" guidance page. Rule source history: 70 FR 50073 (Aug. 25, 2005).

Scope limits: this is the **federal interstate** rule. Intrastate (state-level) passenger-carrier rules can differ; Canadian/Mexican domestic rules are not covered here.

## The three answers

| Ask | Answer | Regulatory basis (quoted) |
|---|---|---|
| 1. How many hours may they drive? | **10 hours** | § 395.5(a)(1): no driver shall drive a passenger-carrying CMV "[m]ore than 10 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty" |
| 2. After how many consecutive hours off duty? | **8 consecutive hours** | § 395.5(a)(1) and (a)(2): both the 10-hour driving limit and the 15-hour on-duty limit run "following 8 consecutive hours off duty" |
| 3. After how many hours on duty may they no longer drive? | **15 hours on duty** | § 395.5(a)(2): no driving "[f]or any period after having been on duty 15 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty" |

Plain language: a passenger-CMV driver may drive **up to 10 hours**, must first take **at least 8 consecutive hours off duty**, and may **not drive after accumulating 15 hours on duty**, counted from the end of that 8-hour off-duty period.

## How the three clocks interlock
- The **8 consecutive hours off duty is the reset**. The 10-hour driving allowance and the 15-hour on-duty window both start from the same point: when the driver comes on duty after 8 consecutive hours off duty.
- The 10 and the 15 are **independent ceilings, not additive**. Whichever binds first controls.
- Worked example: driver comes on duty at 06:00 after 8+ hours off duty. The 15-hour window closes at 21:00. If the driver reaches 10 hours of driving at 19:00, no further driving after 19:00 even though the window is still open. If instead the driver drives only 4 hours but stays on duty (dispatch, waiting, loading, inspections) until 21:00, no further driving after 21:00.
- Consistency: 10 driving hours sits inside the 15-hour on-duty window (10 ≤ 15). No figure above exceeds any limit stated in this answer.
- **Do not import the property-carrier figures.** For property-carrying CMVs the numbers are 11 hours driving / 10 consecutive hours off / 14-hour driving window (§ 395.3). None of those apply to a motorcoach. Note also that the "14 consecutive hours" figure that appears in FMCSA passenger-carrier guidance is the § 395.1(e) short-haul *release-from-duty* period, **not** a driving window.

## Definitions that drive the math (49 CFR 395.2 — read the section for controlling text)
- **Driving time**: all time spent at the driving controls of a CMV in operation.
- **On-duty time**: all time from beginning to end of work — driving, waiting to be dispatched, loading/unloading, inspecting, and any compensated work performed for the carrier or any other employer. Per FMCSA passenger guidance, all compensated work for a motor carrier or non-motor carrier is on-duty time.
- **Off-duty time**: time not on duty, not driving, and not in a sleeper berth.
- The 15-hour clock is **on-duty** time, not driving time. Long passenger stops, delays, and dispatch work burn the window without adding driving hours.

## Weekly ceilings in the same section (outside the three asks, but part of the rule)
§ 395.5(b) bars driving, regardless of how many motor carriers use the driver, after:
- **60 hours on duty in any 7 consecutive days**, if the carrier does **not** operate CMVs every day of the week; or
- **70 hours on duty in any 8 consecutive days**, if the carrier **does** operate CMVs every day of the week.

Multiple-employer drivers: § 395.8(j) — the carrier must obtain a signed statement of the driver's total on-duty time for the preceding 7 days and the time last relieved from duty.

## Exceptions and exemptions under § 395.1 that move the numbers (departures, not the baseline)
- **Sleeper berth — § 395.1(g)(3)**: a driver of a passenger-carrying CMV equipped with a sleeper berth may accumulate the **equivalent of 8 consecutive hours off duty** by taking two rest periods in the sleeper berth, provided the four requirements of § 395.1(g)(3)(i)–(iv) are met. This is a way to *satisfy* the 8-hour requirement, not a change to it. Read the four conditions in the regulation text before applying.
- **Alaska — § 395.1(b)(2), passenger-carrying**: 15 hours driving following 8 consecutive hours off duty; no driving after being on duty 20 hours or more following 8 consecutive hours off duty; 70 hours/7 days or 80 hours/8 days. This is the Alaska variant, not the lower-48 answer.
- **Adverse driving conditions — § 395.1(b)**: relief exists but is bounded; it does not extend the on-duty ceiling. Confirm the exact allowance in the § 395.1(b) text before relying on it.
- **Short-haul — § 395.1(e)**: FMCSA describes a records exemption for drivers operating within a 150 air-mile radius of the normal work reporting location and released from duty within 14 consecutive hours or less. This is a logbook/record-of-duty-status/ELD exception, not a change to the 10 / 8 / 15 limits.
- **Non-business private motor carriers of passengers** are not subject to the Part 395 recordkeeping requirements (e.g., no logbook/RDS) under § 395.8(a)(1), but the driving limits themselves are unchanged.
- **34-hour restart**: the restart language in the current part 395 text sits in the property-carrying section (§ 395.3(c)); confirm its application to passenger carriers against the § 395.1/§ 395.5 text before using it. It does not affect any of the three answers above.

## Common errors this answer is written to prevent
1. Quoting 11 / 10 / 14 (property-carrying) for a motorcoach. Wrong section.
2. Treating the 15 hours as *driving* time. It is *on-duty* time.
3. Treating the 8 hours as sleeper-berth time. It is off-duty time; sleeper berth is only required if the driver is relying on the § 395.1(g)(3) split.
4. Adding the 10 and the 15. They are concurrent ceilings.
5. Applying the 60/70-hour weekly rule without checking the carrier's operating schedule (every day vs. not every day).

## Verification performed
- All three figures are **quoted thresholds**, not derived numbers — no arithmetic or rounding error is possible.
- Cross-source agreement: eCFR § 395.5, govinfo 2025 CFR text, and FMCSA's passenger-carrier guidance page state the identical 10 / 8 / 15 figures.
- Internal consistency: 10 hours driving ≤ 15 hours on duty; the 8-hour off-duty period resets both; no value in this answer violates a limit stated elsewhere in it.
- Applicability check: the vehicle is specified as passenger-carrying (motorcoach), so § 395.5 rather than § 395.3 applies.

The first reads: "(1) More than 10 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty;"

Two pages handed on give different figures for the same thing: 10 on govinfo.gov/content/pkg/cfr-2025-title49-vol5/xml/cfr-2025-title49-vol5-part395.xml and 8 on ecfr.gov/current/title-49/subtitle-b/chapter-iii/subchapter-b/part-395. The first reads: "(A) More than 15 hours following 10 consecutive hours off-duty;"

Two pages handed on give different figures for the same thing: 7 on govinfo.gov/content/pkg/cfr-2025-title49-vol5/xml/cfr-2025-title49-vol5-part395.xml and 8 on ecfr.gov/current/title-49/subtitle-b/chapter-iii/subchapter-b/part-395. The first reads: "(c)(1) Any period of 7 consecutive days may end with the beginning of an off-duty period of 34 or more consecutive hours."

question: M5
answer:
**Answer (default Part 135 flight-attendant rule).** Under 14 CFR 135.273(b)(2), a flight attendant scheduled to a duty period of 14 hours or less must be given a scheduled rest period of at least **9 consecutive hours**. Under 135.273(b)(3), that rest may be **scheduled or reduced to 8 consecutive hours** only if the flight attendant is provided a subsequent rest period of at least **10 consecutive hours**; that 10-hour subsequent rest must be scheduled to begin **no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the reduced rest period** and must occur between completion of the scheduled duty period and commencement of the subsequent duty period.

**Why this is the governing rule.** Section 135.263(e) states that 135.273 prescribes duty period limitations and rest requirements for flight attendants in all operations conducted under Part 135, which includes on-demand charter. Section 135.273(b)(1) caps scheduled duty at 14 hours except for the augmented-crew provisions in (b)(4) through (b)(6). For the 14-hours-or-less tier, (b)(2) and (b)(3) supply the 9-hour baseline and the conditional 8-hour reduction above.

**Conditions and limits.**
- The 9 hours is a minimum, not a maximum; the operator's manual, operations specifications, or collective bargaining agreement may require more.
- The reduced rest is 8 consecutive hours, not less. If the required 10-hour make-up rest cannot be scheduled as required, the 8-hour reduction is not available and the 9-hour minimum applies.
- The 8-hour reduction is not conditioned on a late-night or early-morning termination. The rule's condition is the 10-hour subsequent rest, not the time of day.
- No duty may be assigned during required rest (135.273(b)(11)); no duty period may be assigned unless the flight attendant has had at least the minimum rest required (135.273(b)(10)).
- The 14-hour cap and the 9/8 rest pair apply to scheduled duty of 14 hours or less. A scheduled duty period over 14 hours is outside this answer and must be evaluated under 135.273(b)(4) through (b)(9).
- If the certificate holder has elected the 135.273(c) alternative to apply flight-crewmember rules to flight attendants, the 135.265 rest table governs instead; confirm the operations specifications before using 9/8.

**Scheduling procedure.**
1. Determine the scheduled duty period length. If it is 14.0 hours or less, apply the 9-hour baseline.
2. Schedule at least 9 consecutive hours free of duty between completion of the scheduled duty period and commencement of the next duty period.
3. If an 8-hour rest is operationally desired, schedule 8 consecutive hours free of duty and simultaneously schedule the required 10-consecutive-hour subsequent rest. Verify that the 10-hour rest begins no later than 24 hours after the start of the 8-hour rest.
4. Confirm that the 10-hour rest satisfies the rule's placement requirement: it must occur between completion of the scheduled duty period and commencement of the subsequent duty period. Confirm also that no duty is assigned during either required rest period.
5. If any condition in step 3 or step 4 fails, restore the 9-hour rest.
6. Compare against the company manual, operations specifications, and any collective bargaining agreement; apply the most restrictive requirement.

**Worked timing check.** If the 8-hour reduced rest begins at 22:00, the 10-hour subsequent rest must begin no later than 22:00 the following day. The 10-hour rest must itself be at least 10 consecutive hours. This is a calendar check, not a late-night eligibility check.

**Bottom line.** The flight attendant gets **9 consecutive hours** after a scheduled duty period of 14 hours or less, reducible to **8 consecutive hours** only with a **10-consecutive-hour subsequent rest** beginning within **24 hours** of the start of the reduced rest.

ANSWER (statutory UK minimum wage rates, effective 1 April 2026)

1) National Living Wage (NLW) — workers aged 21 and over: £12.71 per hour.
2) National Minimum Wage (NMW) — 18 to 20 Year Old Rate: £10.85 per hour.

Both are gross hourly amounts in pounds sterling, set by the Government on the recommendation of the Low Pay Commission (LPC) and in force from 1 April 2026. They are the statutory rates, not the voluntary Living Wage Foundation 'Real Living Wage'.

RATE TABLE AS ANNOUNCED (April 2026, for context and to prevent mis-keying)

| Band | April 2026 rate | Annual increase (£) | Annual increase (%) | April 2025 rate |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| National Living Wage (21 and over) | £12.71 | £0.50 | 4.1% | £12.21 |
| 18–20 Year Old Rate | £10.85 | £0.85 | 8.5% | £10.00 |
| 16–17 Year Old Rate | £8.00 | £0.45 | 6.0% | £7.55 |
| Apprentice Rate | £8.00 | £0.45 | 6.0% | £7.55 |

The two asked-for values are the first two rows only. Arithmetic cross-check: 12.21 + 0.50 = 12.71 (4.1%); 10.00 + 0.85 = 10.85 (8.5%). These reconcile exactly with the prior-year figures published on the same gov.uk page, so the numbers are internally consistent.

STATUS / PROVENANCE (for auditability)
- Government acceptance of the LPC recommendations was announced at the Autumn Budget on Wednesday 26 November 2025; the LPC's recommendations were submitted on 27 October 2025.
- The National Minimum Wage (Amendment) Regulations 2026 give the rates legal effect.
- Rates came into force 1 April 2026 and apply to pay reference periods beginning on or after that date.
- Primary sources: gov.uk 'National Minimum Wage rates' (https://www.gov.uk/national-minimum-wage-rates); 'Minimum wage rates for 2026' (https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/minimum-wage-rates-for-2026); 'LPC advice to Government on 2026 minimum wage rates' (https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/minimum-wage-rates-for-2026/lpc-advice-to-government-on-2026-minimum-wage-rates); 'The National Minimum Wage in 2026' (https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/the-national-minimum-wage-in-2026/the-national-minimum-wage-in-2026); LPC press release 'National Living Wage increases to £12.71 per hour' (https://www.gov.uk/government/news/national-living-wage-increases-to-1271-per-hour).

WHAT THIS MEANS IN HR/PAYROLL PRACTICE (the part that is my function)
- Uprating: every worker aged 21+ must be paid at least £12.71 per hour and every worker aged 18–20 at least £10.85 per hour for all hours worked from 1 April 2026. Rates cannot be averaged down across a workforce.
- Age banding: the 21+ threshold for NLW has applied since April 2024 (it was 25+ before April 2021 and 23+ from April 2021). Age is assessed on the worker's age during the pay reference period; a worker turning 21 or 18 moves onto the higher band from the start of the pay reference period in which the birthday falls.
- Salaried and time-based staff: check that monthly salaries divided by contractual hours still clear the new hourly floors, and that deductions (including salary sacrifice, uniforms, tools, accommodation beyond the offset) do not take effective pay below the floor.
- Apprentices: the £8.00 apprentice rate applies only to apprentices aged under 19, or aged 19+ in the first year of their apprenticeship; an apprentice aged 21+ who has completed the first year is entitled to the NLW of £12.71.
- Accommodation: the maximum daily offset for accommodation provided is £11.10 from 1 April 2026.
- Records: keep minimum wage records for at least six years (three years is the statutory minimum in some contexts; six is the safer payroll standard) and retain evidence of the rate applied per worker, so that any arrears or Naming Scheme exposure can be rebutted.
- Named-scheme risk: underpayment of NMW/NLW is a statutory breach carrying arrears at the current rate plus a 200% penalty (capped), so the uprating should be applied at the first pay run on or after 1 April 2026, not deferred.

SCOPE NOTE ON MY ROLE
Setting, interpreting or challenging the statutory rate, the LPC remit, or the two-thirds-of-median-earnings target is policy work outside the HR function — I am reporting the enacted figures and their HR application. question: M11
answer:
COMPLIANCE MEMO — FMCSA SHORT-HAUL EXCEPTION (49 CFR 395.1(e)(1)): RADIUS AND RELEASE WINDOW

1. ANSWERS

1.1 Radius (ask 1): 150 air miles. The driver must operate within a 150 air-mile radius of the normal work reporting location. 49 CFR 395.1(e)(1)(i): 'The driver operates within a 150 air-mile radius (172.6 statute miles) of the normal work reporting location.' The operative measure is AIR miles, not road/statute miles; the regulation supplies 172.6 statute miles only as a conversion parenthetical, not as a separate or alternative limit.

1.2 Release window (ask 2): 14 consecutive hours. The driver must return to the work reporting location and be released from work within 14 consecutive hours. 49 CFR 395.1(e)(1)(ii): 'The driver, except a driver-salesperson, returns to the work reporting location and is released from work within 14 consecutive hours.' The 14 hours run consecutively from the time the driver comes on duty; the count is not paused by off-duty time within the shift.

2. FULL TEXT OF THE CONDITION SET (so the two figures are applied in context)

Under 395.1(e)(1), a driver is exempt from the records-of-duty-status requirement (395.8) and from the supporting-documents requirement (395.11) only if ALL of the following hold:
  (i) operates within a 150 air-mile radius (172.6 statute miles) of the normal work reporting location;
  (ii) except a driver-salesperson, returns to the work reporting location and is released from work within 14 consecutive hours;
  (iii)(A) property-carrying CMV driver: at least 10 consecutive hours off duty separating each 14 hours on duty; (B) passenger-carrying CMV driver: at least 8 consecutive hours off duty separating each 14 hours on duty; and
  (iv) the motor carrier maintains and retains for 6 months accurate and true time records showing, for each day: time the driver reports for duty, total hours on duty, time released from duty, and (for drivers used for the first time or intermittently, per 395.8(j)(2)) total time for the preceding 7 days.

3. SCOPE NOTES — WHAT THESE FIGURES ARE NOT

3.1 Not the non-CDL property-carrying exception (395.1(e)(2)). That separate exception also uses a 150 air-mile radius, but its time structure is different: the driver must return to the normal work reporting location at the end of each duty tour, must not drive after the 14th hour after coming on duty on 5 days of any period of 7 consecutive days, and must not drive after the 16th hour after coming on duty on 2 days of any period of 7 consecutive days. The 14-consecutive-hour release answer in 1.2 is the (e)(1) rule; do not import the (e)(2) 16-hour allowance into an (e)(1) analysis.

3.2 Not the 16-hour exception (395.1(o)). The 16-hour window (return to normal work reporting location and release within 16 hours after coming on duty following 10 consecutive hours off duty, subject to the prior-five-duty-tour and once-per-6-days conditions) is a distinct exception and does not enlarge the (e)(1) 14-hour release window.

3.3 Not the motion-picture exception (395.1(p)). That provision uses a 100 air-mile radius for transportation to or from a motion picture production site. It is unrelated to the short-haul RODS exception and its 100-mile figure must not be used to answer ask 1.

3.4 Not the pre-2020 rule. Before the 2020 hours-of-service final rule, the short-haul exception was a 100 air-mile radius with a 12-hour release window. Those figures are superseded. The current text quoted above (150 air miles / 14 consecutive hours) is the one to apply; both the eCFR current text and the 2024 printed CFR agree.

4. OPERATIONAL CONSEQUENCES (compliance-relevant, stated so the figures are usable)

4.1 Measurement. Radius compliance is tested in straight-line (air) miles from the normal work reporting location to the driver's furthest point of operation, not by route mileage. A driver whose road route exceeds 150 miles but whose air-mile displacement never exceeds 150 remains within the radius on that element.

4.2 Location identity. The driver must start and end the shift at the same reporting location. FMCSA guidance states that the start/end location may differ from shift to shift so long as each individual shift starts and ends at the same place; the 150 air-mile radius is measured from that shift's normal work reporting location.

4.3 Loss of the exception for the day. If the driver exceeds the 150 air-mile radius or is not released within 14 consecutive hours on a given day, the exception is unavailable for that day and the driver must complete a record of duty status for the day (paper log, or ELD if the driver is otherwise required to use one). A driver required to complete a log more than 8 days within the last 30 days must use an ELD to record time for that day.

4.4 Driver-salesperson carve-out. The 14-consecutive-hour release condition in (e)(1)(ii) expressly excepts a driver-salesperson; the radius condition is unaffected.

4.5 Recordkeeping is a condition, not a formality. The 6-month time records in (e)(1)(iv) — report time, total hours on duty, release time, plus 7-day totals for new/intermittent drivers — must exist and be accurate for the exemption to be supportable on audit.

5. AUTHORITY

49 CFR 395.1(e)(1)(i) (150 air-mile radius; 172.6 statute miles) and 395.1(e)(1)(ii) (return and release within 14 consecutive hours), as published in the current eCFR text of section 395.1 and in the 2024 edition of 49 CFR, volume 5; consistent with FMCSA's Summary of Hours of Service Regulations ('operates within a 150 air-mile radius of the normal work reporting location, and ... does not exceed a maximum duty period of 14 hours') and FMCSA's short-haul training material ('Operate within a 150 air-mile radius ... Not exceed a maximum duty period of 14 hours').

question: H1
answer:
COMPLIANCE ANSWER — Minimum rest between duty days for a US airline flight attendant

1. THE NUMBER

At least 10 consecutive hours.

For a US-domiciled air carrier operating under 14 CFR Part 121 (domestic, flag, and supplemental operations), a flight attendant scheduled to a duty period of 14 hours or less must be given a scheduled rest period of at least 10 consecutive hours between the completion of one scheduled duty period and the commencement of the next. The rest period may not be reduced below 10 consecutive hours under any circumstances.

2. REGULATORY BASIS

- 14 CFR §121.467(b)(2), as amended: 'A flight attendant scheduled to a duty period of 14 hours or less as provided under paragraph (b)(1) of this section must be given a scheduled rest period of at least 10 consecutive hours. This rest period must occur between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period.'
- 14 CFR §121.467(b)(3), as amended: 'The rest period required under paragraph (b)(2) of this section may not be reduced to less than 10 consecutive hours.'
- Statutory driver: §335(a) of the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2018 (Pub. L. 115-254), which directed the FAA to set the minimum rest period at not less than 10 consecutive hours for a flight attendant scheduled for a duty period of 14 hours or less and to prohibit reduction of that rest period under any circumstances.
- Implementing final rule: FAA, 'Flight Attendant Duty Period Limitations and Rest Requirements' (docket document ARM-220928-001), issued on or about 4 October 2022, amending §121.467(b)(2) and (b)(3). The rule was published in the Federal Register on 4 October 2022 and took effect 30 days after publication. (Verify the exact Federal Register citation and effective date against the published rule before using either in a filing or training document — the source file confirms the issuance date but not the effective date.)

3. WHAT CHANGED (do not use the old numbers)

- Before the 2022 amendment, §121.467(b)(2) required 9 consecutive hours, and §121.467(b)(3) permitted that to be scheduled or reduced to 8 consecutive hours if followed by a subsequent rest of at least 10 consecutive hours beginning no later than 24 hours after the start of the reduced rest. That 9/8 regime is repealed for Part 121.
- The 9-hour and 8-hour figures still appear in the FAA's public FAQ page and in 14 CFR §§91.1062 and 135.273. Those are (i) a stale web page that restates the pre-2022 rule and (ii) different regulatory parts that do not govern a Part 121 scheduled airline. Do not cite them for a Part 121 carrier.
- Practical effect: any airline schedule, bid package, or crew-tracking rule that still builds an 8-hour reduced-rest layover into a Part 121 flight attendant pairing is non-compliant as of the rule's effective date.

4. CONDITIONS AND DEFINITIONS THAT MATTER IN PRACTICE

- 'Consecutive' is literal: the clock runs from completion of the scheduled duty period to commencement of the subsequent duty period, and it must be a single uninterrupted block of at least 10 hours.
- No reduction, no waiver, no 'make-up rest' mechanism. Unlike the pre-2022 rule, there is no provision allowing the carrier to trade a shorter rest period now for a longer one later.
- No duty during rest: the carrier may not assign a flight attendant to any duty during a required rest period, and may not assign a duty period unless the flight attendant has had at least the minimum rest. (This is stated in terms in the parallel §§135.273(b)(10)–(11) and 91.1062 text; §121.467 contains the analogous prohibition — confirm the paragraph numbering against the current eCFR text before quoting a paragraph letter.)
- Non-local transportation does not count as rest. Time the carrier requires and provides to move a flight attendant to a distant airport to serve a flight, or home from a point of release, is not part of the rest period (again, see the parallel §135.273(b)(12) language; confirm the §121.467 analog). Local hotel-to-airport transportation at a layover is ordinarily inside the rest period and does not extend it — but this is the single most common source of short-rest violations, so scheduling systems should measure rest from actual block-in/release, not scheduled release.
- Weekly floor: the carrier must relieve each flight attendant from all further duty for at least 24 consecutive hours during any 7 consecutive calendar days (parallel provision; confirm §121.467 paragraph).

5. THE EXTENDED-DUTY VARIANT (do not confuse with the headline answer)

Where the carrier lawfully assigns a duty period longer than 14 hours (permitted only with additional flight attendants above the minimum complement, up to 20 hours), the required rest rises to at least 12 consecutive hours. The 2022 rule amended only paragraphs (b)(2) and (b)(3) of §121.467, so the 12-hour tier and its reduction provision remain in the regulatory text as amended. Two cautions: (i) the 12-hour figure applies only to extended duty periods and must never be presented as the general between-duty-days minimum; (ii) the residual reduction provision in that tier (to 10 consecutive hours with a subsequent 14-hour rest) is in tension with the statute's 'prohibit reduction under any circumstances' direction, so treat the reduction as unusable unless legal counsel confirms otherwise against the current eCFR text and any later rulemaking. For the ordinary case — duty period of 14 hours or less — the answer is 10 hours, full stop.

6. WHAT THE NUMBER IS NOT

- Not the Part 117 pilot rule. Part 117 flight/duty/rest limits apply to flight crewmembers, not cabin crew. The coincidence that Part 117's minimum rest is also 10 hours is coincidental and does not support cross-citation.
- Not Part 135 or Part 91 subpart K. Those parts still carry the 9-hour requirement with an 8-hour reduction option (§§135.273(b)(2)–(3), 91.1062(a)(2)–(3)). A commuter or fractional operator is governed by those, not by §121.467.
- Not a ceiling. The 10-hour figure is the federal floor. Collective bargaining agreements at most major US carriers exceed it (commonly 11–12 hours, with contractual rest measured from actual release and with hotel-quality and transportation protections), and some state laws or local ordinances add requirements. The binding obligation is whichever is more restrictive: the FAR, the CBA, or applicable state law.
- Not a rule about reserve, delays, or irregular operations. Rest after an unscheduled delay or a mid-duty interruption is governed by the same §121.467 rest requirement applied to the actual (not scheduled) completion of duty, plus the carrier's FAA-approved/ops-spec procedures; do not answer a delay question with the scheduled-rest figure alone.

7. VERIFICATION CHECKLIST BEFORE THIS GOES INTO A MANUAL OR A FILING

1. Pull 14 CFR §121.467 from eCFR (current) and confirm (b)(2) reads '10 consecutive hours' and (b)(3) reads 'may not be reduced to less than 10 consecutive hours.'
2. Confirm no post-2022 rulemaking has further amended §121.467 (check the eCFR 'authority' and source notes, and the FAA's recent final rules).
3. Confirm the exact Federal Register citation and effective date of the 4 October 2022 final rule.
4. Confirm paragraph numbering for the no-duty-during-rest, non-local-transportation, and 24-in-7 provisions in §121.467 before quoting them by paragraph.
5. Confirm the applicable CBA rest article and any state-law overlay; adopt the most restrictive.
6. Purge any internal schedule-building or crew-tracking rule that still permits an 8-hour reduced-rest layover, and audit pairings built under the pre-2022 rule.

CURRENT US NATIONAL PRIMARY (HEALTH-BASED) PM2.5 NAAQS

Answer
- Annual primary PM2.5 standard: 9.0 µg/m³ (micrograms per cubic meter), annual arithmetic mean concentration.
- 24-hour primary PM2.5 standard: 35 µg/m³, 24-hour average concentration.

Both are mass concentrations; PM2.5 standards are expressed only in µg/m³. There is no ppm/ppb form for PM (ppb/ppm expressions apply to gaseous NAAQS such as NO2, SO2 and CO), so no dual-unit statement is applicable.

Regulatory form (stated so the levels are not misread)
| Standard | Level | Indicator | Averaging time | Form (40 CFR part 50, appendix N) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Primary annual PM2.5 | 9.0 µg/m³ | PM2.5 | 1 year | Annual arithmetic mean, averaged over 3 years; level defined to one decimal place |
| Primary 24-hour PM2.5 | 35 µg/m³ | PM2.5 | 24 hours | Annual 98th percentile of 24-hour concentrations, averaged over 3 years; level defined as an integer |

Rounding conventions (from EPA's NAAQS timeline footnotes and appendix N): the annual level is compared to a 3-year average of annual means rounded to one decimal place (e.g., 9.04 rounds to 9.0 and meets 9.0; 9.05 rounds to 9.1 and violates 9.0). The 24-hour level is compared to a 3-year average of annual 98th percentiles rounded to an integer (e.g., 35.49 rounds to 35 and meets 35; 35.50 rounds to 36 and violates 35).

Legal basis and effective date
- 40 CFR 50.20, 'National primary ambient air quality standards for PM2.5', added by 'Reconsideration of the National Ambient Air Quality Standards for Particulate Matter', 89 FR 16202 (March 6, 2024), effective May 6, 2024. Section 50.20(a) sets 9.0 µg/m³ annual arithmetic mean and 35 µg/m³ 24-hour average; 50.20(b) and (c) give the met conditions at 9.0 and 35 respectively.
- EPA's PM NAAQS timeline confirms the 2024 row: Primary, PM2.5, 1 year, 9.0 µg/m³, annual arithmetic mean averaged over 3 years, with 'all other primary and secondary PM2.5 and PM10 standards retained without revision.'
- The 24-hour primary standard of 35 µg/m³ dates to the 2006 review (71 FR 61224) and was retained without revision in 2012 (78 FR 3085), 2020 (85 FR 82684) and 2024 (89 FR 16202).

As-of basis
'Current' is taken to mean the standards in effect under the latest finalized EPA PM NAAQS rule as of the source retrieval date of these records (2026-11-16): the 2024 reconsideration rule, effective May 6, 2024. The values above are the ones in force on that basis.

Disambiguation notes (why a reader may see 15.0 µg/m³ and should not report it as the primary annual level)
1. 40 CFR 50.13 still contains 15.0 µg/m³ annual and 35 µg/m³ 24-hour. Section 50.13(d) provides that the 1997 primary annual standard 'will no longer apply' upon the effective date of the PM SIP-requirements rule, while the 1997 secondary annual standard and the 1997 24-hour PM2.5 standard remain in effect. Thus 15.0 µg/m³ survives as the secondary (welfare-based) annual standard, not as the primary annual standard. The 2012 primary annual standard of 12.0 µg/m³ (40 CFR 50.18) was superseded by the 2024 level of 9.0 µg/m³.
2. Secondary standards: the secondary annual PM2.5 standard remains 15.0 µg/m³; the 24-hour PM2.5 standard (35 µg/m³) is both primary and secondary and was retained unchanged in 2024 and again in the December 2024 secondary-standards action (89 FR 105692). Only the primary annual level changed in 2024.
3. The 24-hour primary level is 35 µg/m³, not the 1997-era 65 µg/m³.

Watch item (does not change the answer above)
The EPA PM NAAQS page carries a March 12, 2025 announcement of a 'Path Forward' on the PM2.5 standards. No finalized rule revising the 9.0 µg/m³ annual or 35 µg/m³ 24-hour primary levels appears in the sources reviewed; if such a rule is later finalized, the annual level (and only that level, on current information) would be the figure to re-verify against 40 CFR 50.20 and the Federal Register before reuse. The values reported here should therefore be cited with their effective date (May 6, 2024) rather than as undated facts.
