SAFETY ENGINEERING ANSWER — General-industry fall-protection trigger height, walking-working surfaces with unprotected sides or edges (federal OSHA, 29 CFR 1910 Subpart D)

1. BOTTOM LINE

A US employer in general industry (not construction) must protect each employee on a walking-working surface with an unprotected side or edge that is 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level.

Answer: 4 feet (1.2 m), measured from the walking-working surface down to the lower level.

The threshold is inclusive. At exactly 4 feet, protection is required. The regulatory language is "4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level," not "more than 4 feet."

2. CONTROLLING CITATION AND TEXT

29 CFR 1910.28(b)(1)(i) — "Unprotected sides and edges":

"Except as provided elsewhere in this section, the employer must ensure that each employee on a walking-working surface with an unprotected side or edge that is 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level is protected from falling by one or more of the following:
(A) Guardrail systems;
(B) Safety net systems; or
(C) Personal fall protection systems, such as personal fall arrest, travel restraint, or positioning systems."

Supporting scope provision: 29 CFR 1910.28(a)(1) makes the section applicable to walking-working surfaces in general industry workplaces, with the carve-outs in 1910.28(a)(2) (powered platforms under 1910.66(j); aerial lifts under 1910.67(c)(2)(v); telecommunications work under 1910.268(n)(7) and (8); electric power generation, transmission, and distribution work under 1910.269(g)(2)(i)). Those carve-outs are not a different height — they simply move the requirement to the cited section.

3. HOW THE 4-FOOT TRIGGER IS MEASURED AND WHEN IT APPLIES

- Measurement datum: vertical distance from the walking-working surface on which the employee stands to the next lower level. "Lower level" is not limited to grade; a floor, mezzanine, roof below, pit, tank, or water surface can be the lower level.
- "Unprotected side or edge": an open side or edge of a floor, roof, balcony/deck, platform, ramp, runway, or other walking-working surface that lacks a guardrail system or an equivalent barrier (e.g., a parapet of adequate strength). Entrances and points of access are not treated as unprotected edges.
- "Walking-working surface": any horizontal or vertical surface on or through which an employee walks, works, or gains access to a work area — floors, ground, roofs, ramps, bridges, runways, stairs, dockboards, formwork, reinforcing steel; ladders are excluded from the definition and are governed separately.
- The lead-in phrase "Except as provided elsewhere in this section" matters: where a more specific paragraph of 1910.28 addresses the surface, that paragraph controls (see the table in section 5).
- The trigger is a duty-to-protect height; it is independent of which of the three permitted protection methods the employer selects. Method selection is a separate design decision under 1910.28(b)(1)(i)(A)-(C) and the performance criteria in 1910.29 (guardrail geometry and strength, safety net criteria, personal fall protection system criteria).
- Employee training on fall hazards and the protection systems in use is required by 29 CFR 1910.30.

4. PERMITTED PROTECTION METHODS AT THE 4-FOOT TRIGGER

Any one or more of: (A) guardrail systems; (B) safety net systems; (C) personal fall protection systems — personal fall arrest, travel restraint, or positioning systems.

Related general-industry alternative for residential roofs: under 1910.28(b)(1)(ii), where the employer can demonstrate that guardrail, safety net, or personal fall protection systems are infeasible or create a greater hazard on residential roofs, the employer must implement a fall protection plan meeting 29 CFR 1926.502(k) plus training meeting 29 CFR 1926.503(a) and (c). This is a documented-infeasibility exception, not a different trigger height.

5. SURFACES WITH THE SAME OR A DIFFERENT TRIGGER (so the 4-foot answer is applied correctly)

Same 4-foot (1.2 m) trigger, stated in the specific paragraph:
- Holes (including skylights) an employee can fall through — 1910.28(b)(3); protection by covers, guardrails, travel restraint, or personal fall arrest.
- Dockboards — 1910.28(b)(4)(i): guardrail system or handrails at 4 feet or more. Narrow exception at 1910.28(b)(4)(ii): guardrails/handrails not required when the dockboard is used solely for materials handling with motorized equipment, employees are not exposed to fall hazards greater than 10 feet (3 m), and employees are trained under 1910.30.
- Runways and similar walkways — 1910.28(b)(5)(i): guardrail system at 4 feet or more; the one-sided-guardrail allowance in (b)(5)(ii) still requires a personal fall arrest or travel restraint system for each employee.
- Stairway landings — 1910.28(b)(11)(i).
- Slaughtering facility platforms (unprotected working side) — 1910.28(b)(14)(i): guardrail or travel restraint at 4 feet or more.
- Walking-working surfaces not otherwise addressed — 1910.28(b)(15): 4 feet or more; guardrail, safety net, or personal fall protection.
- Low-slope roofs — 1910.28(b)(13): the 4-foot trigger applies, but this paragraph permits additional protection methods (e.g., warning line systems, designated areas, safety monitoring) at greater heights and imposes specific work-rule conditions. Verify the paragraph's height tiers against the current regulatory text before finalizing a roof-specific plan; they are not reproduced here.

Different trigger (do not substitute these for the 4-foot answer):
- Dangerous equipment — 1910.28(b)(6): protection required regardless of height where an employee is exposed to a fall into or onto dangerous equipment (vats, tanks, electrical equipment, machinery with protruding parts, or similar).
- Scaffolds — 29 CFR 1910.27(a) incorporates 29 CFR 1926.450, .451, .452, and .454; fall protection for scaffold work is triggered at 10 feet under 1926.451(g)(1). Scaffold trigger heights therefore sit above the 4-foot walking-working-surface rule.
- Fixed ladders — 1910.28(b)(9)(i): a personal fall arrest system or ladder safety system is required for fixed ladders extending more than 24 feet above a lower level (with the paragraph's phase-in/retrofit provisions and cage/well conditions). This is an additional ladder requirement, not a modification of the 4-foot edge rule.
- Stair rails and handrails — 1910.28(b)(11)(ii): required for each flight of stairs having at least 3 treads and 4 risers, independent of the 4-foot fall-protection trigger.

6. GENERAL INDUSTRY VS. CONSTRUCTION (explicit contrast, since construction was excluded)

- General industry (this answer): 4 feet (1.2 m) — 29 CFR 1910.28(b)(1)(i).
- Construction: 6 feet (1.8 m) — 29 CFR 1926.501(b)(1), plus the construction-specific triggers for excavations (6 feet), wall openings, and established floors where non-construction employees would instead be protected at 4 feet.

The 4-foot figure governs only when the work is general industry under 29 CFR Part 1910. Work that is construction work under 29 CFR 1926.501 is governed by the 6-foot figure. If a site has both, classify the task correctly before choosing a threshold.

7. STATE-PLAN JURISDICTION CAVEAT

Federal OSHA sets the floor. OSHA-approved state plans (e.g., Washington, Oregon, and other state-plan jurisdictions) must be at least as effective as federal OSHA and may adopt different or stricter requirements. In the material reviewed, Washington's rule is also 4 feet or more (WAC 296-880-20005(1), "walking/working surfaces with unprotected sides or edges ... four feet or more above the ground or lower level"), and Oregon OSHA's trigger-height fact sheet (FS-58) lists unprotected sides and edges at 4 feet (1910.28(b)(1)) with dangerous equipment at any height. Where the workplace is in a state-plan state, confirm the state standard and any state-specific trigger heights (for example, Washington requires protection for holes, impalement hazards, and work above or adjacent to dangerous equipment regardless of height) before relying on the federal figure alone.

8. HOW THIS ANSWER WAS VERIFIED / LIMITS

- The 4-foot figure is taken directly from the regulatory text of 29 CFR 1910.28(b)(1)(i) as published on eCFR, and is corroborated by Oregon OSHA FS-58, which lists "Unprotected sides and edges — X — 1910.28(b)(1)" (X = required at heights equal to or greater than the listed height).
- The answer is jurisdiction-general and surface-general by design: it states the trigger height for unprotected sides and edges of walking-working surfaces. It does not perform a workplace-specific hazard assessment, does not select a protection method for a particular task, and does not resolve the correct classification of a mixed general-industry/construction site. Those require site-specific review.
- Practical application rule for a safety program: treat 4 feet (1.2 m) as the design and audit threshold for guardrails, covers, travel restraint, or fall arrest on any walking-working surface with an open side or edge, escalate to protection regardless of height where the fall would be into or onto dangerous equipment, and document any reliance on a paragraph-specific alternative (residential-roof fall protection plan, dockboard materials-handling exception, one-sided runway guardrail).

REGULATORY ANSWER — VFR RESERVE FUEL, US-REGISTERED HELICOPTER

1. THE VALUE

A helicopter beginning a VFR flight in the United States must carry enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and then, assuming normal cruising speed, to fly for at least 20 minutes beyond that point. The reserve is therefore 20 minutes of flight time at normal cruising speed. It is a time-based minimum, not a fixed quantity of fuel; the gallon or pound figure is derived per aircraft.

There is no day/night distinction. Twenty minutes applies to day VFR and night VFR alike.

2. PRIMARY CITATION — 14 CFR 91.151(b)

Section 91.151, 'Fuel requirements for flight in VFR conditions,' reads in paragraph (b):

'No person may begin a flight in a rotorcraft under VFR conditions unless (considering wind and forecast weather conditions) there is enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising speed, to fly after that for at least 20 minutes.'

The contrast with paragraph (a) is the whole point and is worth stating because it is the most common source of error: paragraph (a) covers airplanes and requires 30 minutes during the day and 45 minutes at night. Those two figures do not apply to rotorcraft. A helicopter pilot who applies the airplane numbers is over-planning (harmless), and a pilot who applies 30/45 as if they were the helicopter rule has misread the regulation.

3. THE NUMBER DOES NOT CHANGE UNDER PART 135

For a helicopter operated commercially under 14 CFR Part 135, 135.209(b) is textually parallel:

'No person may begin a flight operation in a helicopter under VFR unless, considering wind and forecast weather conditions, it has enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising fuel consumption, to fly after that for at least 20 minutes.'

So the 20-minute figure is the answer whether the flight is Part 91 or Part 135. The only wording difference is that 91.151(b) says 'normal cruising speed' and 135.209(b) says 'normal cruising fuel consumption' — operationally the same computation, since time at cruise speed converts to fuel via the cruise burn rate.

Part 121 is an airplane regime and does not govern helicopter operations, so there is no third figure to reconcile.

4. WHAT THIS RESERVE IS NOT (SCOPE LIMITS)

- It is not an IFR figure. Under IFR the helicopter numbers are different: 91.167(a)(3) requires 45 minutes at normal cruising speed after the alternate, or 30 minutes for helicopters; 135.223(a)(3) likewise requires 30 minutes for helicopters. Those 30-minute figures are IFR and do not apply to a VFR flight. Do not substitute them.
- It is not an alternate-airport requirement. VFR reserve fuel under 91.151(b) is computed to the first point of intended landing only; there is no regulatory VFR alternate fuel add-on for helicopters.
- It is not a maximum-endurance figure. The 20 minutes is flown at normal cruising speed, not at best-endurance airspeed, so it should be computed at the cruise power setting and cruise fuel flow actually planned.
- It is a floor, not a target. 91.151(b) sets the minimum to begin the flight; it does not license planning to land with exactly 20 minutes remaining. Operators, insurers, and good practice routinely impose more, particularly over water, at night, in mountainous terrain, or where weather is forecast to deteriorate.

5. CONVERTING 20 MINUTES TO A FUEL QUANTITY

Procedure:

  Step 1. Establish the planned normal cruise speed (Vno/Vh or the speed the flight will actually be flown) and the corresponding cruise fuel flow from the aircraft's performance data — gallons per hour or pounds per hour.
  Step 2. Reserve fuel = cruise fuel flow x (20 / 60) = cruise fuel flow / 3.
  Step 3. Add unusable fuel and any fuel not reachable in the tank/system configuration, because the reserve must be usable fuel. Confirm against the aircraft's usable-fuel figure, not total tank capacity.
  Step 4. Total fuel at start = trip fuel to first point of intended landing (computed with wind and forecast temperature) + reserve from Step 2 + taxi/run-up/start allowance + any operator or PIC discretionary margin.

Worked examples (illustrative, verify against the specific aircraft's performance data):

- Turbine helicopter burning 120 lb/hr at normal cruise: reserve = 120 / 3 = 40 lb. At roughly 6.7 lb/gal for Jet A that is about 6.0 gal.
- Piston helicopter burning 13 gal/hr at normal cruise (R44-class): reserve = 13 / 3 = approximately 4.3 gal.
- Piston helicopter burning 9 gal/hr at normal cruise: reserve = 9 / 3 = 3.0 gal.

Because the rule is time-based, the fuel quantity that satisfies it changes with power setting and density altitude; the 20-minute clock does not.

6. RELATED DUTIES THAT BOUND THE ANSWER

- 91.103 requires the pilot in command to become familiar with all available information before flight, including fuel requirements — the 20-minute reserve is part of that preflight determination, not a post-departure adjustment.
- 91.3 makes the PIC directly responsible for, and the final authority as to, the operation — including the decision to carry more than the regulatory minimum.
- 91.151(b) governs the fuel state at the moment the flight begins ('begin a flight'). The reserve must be aboard at takeoff, and it must be preserved in flight; burning into it before reaching the first point of intended landing is a violation of the planning requirement the rule imposes.
- Certain specialized helicopter operations (external-load under Part 133, agricultural under Part 137) obtain relief from specified Part 91 subparts; where such relief applies, confirm the fuel-planning rule that remains in force. Absent specific relief, 91.151(b) is the baseline.

7. ONE-LINE ANSWER FOR THE RECORD

Twenty minutes of flight time at normal cruising speed, computed beyond the fuel needed to reach the first point of intended landing, per 14 CFR 91.151(b) for Part 91 operations and 14 CFR 135.209(b) for Part 135 helicopter operations; identical for day and night VFR; not to be confused with the 30-minute airplane-day, 45-minute airplane-night, or 30-minute helicopter-IFR figures.

# Deprecation of TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 — citation and resulting status

## Answers

1. **The RFC that deprecated TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 is RFC 8996**, *Deprecating TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1* (Moriarty & Farrell; March 2021; part of BCP 195; Status of This Memo: "This memo documents an Internet Best Current Practice").

2. **It moved the RFCs that defined those versions to Historic status.** RFC 2246 (TLS 1.0) and RFC 4346 (TLS 1.1) were moved to Historic. The action taken is a status change to *Historic*, not an obsoletion by RFC 8996 — see the note in §3 below, because conflating "obsoleted" with "moved to Historic" is the most common error in restating this answer.

## 1. The deprecating document

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| RFC number | RFC 8996 |
| Title | Deprecating TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 |
| Authors | K. Moriarty, S. Farrell |
| Publication date | March 2021 (Datatracker records RFC 8996 as 2021-03-23) |
| Stream / status | IETF; Internet Best Current Practice — part of BCP 195 |
| Obsoletes | (none) |
| Updates | RFC 7525 (TLS best practices) and a long list of RFCs that normatively reference TLS 1.0/1.1, as enumerated in the document |
| Working group | TLS (draft-ietf-tls-oldversions-deprecate) |

Grounded text (RFC 8996 Abstract, rfc-editor.org):

> "This document formally deprecates Transport Layer Security (TLS) versions 1.0 (RFC 2246) and 1.1 (RFC 4346). Accordingly, those documents have been moved to Historic status."

## 2. Status assigned to the defining RFCs

| Protocol version | Defining RFC | Status after RFC 8996 |
|---|---|---|
| TLS 1.0 | RFC 2246 | Historic |
| TLS 1.1 | RFC 4346 | Historic |
| DTLS 1.0 (also deprecated by RFC 8996) | RFC 4347 | Historic |
| DTLS 1.2 | RFC 6347 | Not deprecated (still current at the time; RFC 8996 only *updates* it to forbid negotiating DTLS 1.0) |

Grounded text (RFC 8996, §1 Introduction):

> "Transport Layer Security (TLS) versions 1.0 [RFC2246] and 1.1 [RFC4346] were superseded by TLS 1.2 [RFC5246] in 2008, which has now itself been superseded by TLS 1.3 [RFC8446]. Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS) version 1.0 [RFC4347] was superseded by DTLS 1.2 [RFC6347] in 2012. Therefore, it is timely to further deprecate TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1, and DTLS 1.0. **Accordingly, the aforementioned documents have been moved to Historic status.**"

RFC 8996 additionally moved RFC 5469 (DES/IDEA cipher suites for TLS) to Historic, because the only TLS versions for which those suites were defined are now Historic. It also marks RFC 7507 (version-fallback SCSV) as superseded, and forbids negotiation of DTLS 1.0 in RFC 6347.

## 3. Precision note — "Historic" is not "obsoleted"

The two actions are distinct and must not be merged in any restatement:

- **Obsoletion** of RFC 2246 happened earlier, by RFC 4346 (TLS 1.1); RFC 4346 was in turn obsoleted by RFC 5246 (TLS 1.2). Those obsoletions are recorded in the "Obsoletes" header of those documents, not in RFC 8996.
- **RFC 8996 does not list RFC 2246 or RFC 4346 in its own "Obsoletes" header.** Its action on them is a status change: they are *moved to Historic*. RFC 8996 is a Best Current Practice that documents the deprecation and records the status change.

So the correct sentence is: *"RFC 8996 formally deprecates TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 and moves RFC 2246 and RFC 4346 to Historic status."* A sentence of the form *"RFC 8996 obsoletes RFC 2246 and RFC 4346"* is wrong on both counts — wrong verb, and wrong attribution of which document did the obsoleting.

## 4. Scope caveats worth carrying with the answer

- **Deprecation ≠ removal.** RFC 8996 changes IETF status and recommends against use; it does not delete the protocol versions, the cipher-suite registry entries, or existing implementations. The document notes that registry entries for no-longer-desirable cipher suites remain in the registries, though many TLS registries were updated by RFC 8447 to mark them not recommended.
- **Motivation.** Stated technical reasons: mandatory-to-implement older cipher suites (e.g., TLS 1.0 makes TLS_DHE_DSS_WITH_3DES_EDE_CBC_SHA mandatory), lack of AEAD cipher support before TLS 1.2, handshake integrity dependent on SHA-1, and peer authentication dependent on SHA-1 signatures. Non-technical pressure cited: government and industry profiles (the draft versions cite, among others, the Canadian government treasury board) mandating avoidance of these versions.
- **Not a vendor or regulatory action.** PCI-DSS, browser, and operator deprecations of TLS 1.0/1.1 are separate from, and not citable as, the IETF deprecation. The IETF action is RFC 8996 alone.
- **Status of RFC 8996 itself.** It is an Internet Best Current Practice (BCP 195), not a Proposed Standard. It updates RFC 7525 and thereby joins BCP 195.

## 5. One-line citation form

> Moriarty, K. and S. Farrell, "Deprecating TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1", BCP 195, RFC 8996, DOI 10.17487/RFC8996, March 2021, <https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc8996/>.

Use with: *"RFC 8996 formally deprecates TLS 1.0 (RFC 2246) and TLS 1.1 (RFC 4346), and moves both documents to Historic status."*

ANSWER

The US Social Security contribution and benefit base (the OASDI taxable maximum — the maximum amount of earnings subject to the Social Security payroll tax) for calendar year 2026 is $184,500.

This is the officially announced figure, not a projection. It applies to wages and self-employment income earned in 2026 and is stated in whole US dollars, as SSA publishes it.

STATUTORY BASIS

Under the Social Security Act, the base for any year Y after 1994 equals the 1994 base of $60,600 multiplied by the ratio of the national average wage index for year (Y-2) to that for 1992, rounded to the nearest multiple of $300, and never reduced below the prior year's base. The formula applies only in years for which a December cost-of-living increase is effective. SSA's Office of the Chief Actuary publishes the resulting figure each autumn for the following year.

Verification of the rounding rule against the stated value: $184,500 / $300 = 615 exactly, so $184,500 is a valid statutory multiple of $300. It also exceeds the 2025 base of $176,100, satisfying the no-reduction clause.

PRIMARY SOURCE CORROBORATION (five independent SSA pages, all agreeing)

1. SSA 2026 COLA Fact Sheet (ssa.gov/cola/factsheets/2026.html) — table "Maximum Taxable Earnings": Social Security (OASDI only) 2025 = $176,100; 2026 = $184,500; Medicare (HI only) = No Limit.
2. SSA Fast Facts & Figures About Social Security, 2026 (ssa.gov/policy/docs/chartbooks/fast_facts/2026/fast_facts26.html) — "Maximum earnings subject to Social Security taxes, 2026 (in dollars): OASDI 184,500; HI No limit."
3. SSA Maximum Taxable Earnings history page (ssa.gov/benefits/retirement/planner/maxtax.html) — year table ends 2025 = $176,100; 2026 = $184,500.
4. SSA FAQ KA-02387, dated January 2, 2026 (ssa.gov/faqs/en/questions/KA-02387.html) — "In 2026, the maximum amount of earnings on which you must pay Social Security tax is $184,500. ... There is no maximum earnings amount for Medicare tax."
5. SSA Office of the Chief Actuary, Contribution and Benefit Base (ssa.gov/oact/cola/cbb.html) — history table: 2025 = $176,100; 2026 = $184,500; 2027 = $192,300.

Indirect corroboration: SSA's Contribution and Benefit Base Determination page (ssa.gov/oact/cola/cbbdet.html) computes the 2027 base as the larger of the formula result ($192,300) and "the 2026 base of $184,500," i.e., SSA itself uses $184,500 as the settled 2026 base.

WHAT THIS MEANS IN PRACTICE (derived arithmetic, shown so it can be checked)

- Employee OASDI withholding: 6.2% on earnings up to $184,500. Maximum employee contribution for 2026 = $184,500 x 0.062 = $11,439.00.
- Employer OASDI contribution: same 6.2% and same $11,439.00 maximum per employee.
- Combined employer + employee maximum = $11,439.00 x 2 = $22,878.00.
- Self-employed: 12.4% OASDI on net self-employment income up to $184,500. Maximum OASDI self-employment contribution for 2026 = $184,500 x 0.124 = $22,878.00 (the deductible-half and SECA mechanics affect income tax, not this OASDI cap).
- Medicare (HI): 1.45% employee / 1.45% employer / 2.9% self-employed applies to all earnings — there is no HI wage base. The additional 0.9% Medicare tax above $200,000 single / $250,000 married-filing-jointly is separate and not part of the 7.65% combined rate.
- Earnings above $184,500 in 2026 are not subject to OASDI tax, and $184,500 is also the maximum amount of 2026 earnings that can be credited in a Social Security benefit computation.
- If an individual holds multiple jobs, each employer withholds on its own payroll and total withholding can exceed the cap; the excess is recoverable as a credit when filing the federal return.
- Context for scale: the 2025 base was $176,100, so the 2026 base rises $8,400, or about 4.77%. This is driven by the national average wage index and is distinct from the 2.8% COLA also effective for 2026.

SCOPE NOTES

- The question asks for the OASDI (Social Security) base only; the Medicare wage base is unlimited and is mentioned solely to prevent confusion.
- Other 2026 parameters announced alongside it (quarter of coverage $1,890; retirement earnings test $24,480/yr under FRA and $65,160/yr in the FRA year; SGA $1,690 non-blind / $2,830 blind; maximum benefit at FRA $4,152/mo) are not part of the answer and are listed only as cross-checks that the same official announcement is the source.
- The figure is final and officially published; no projection, forecast, or estimate is involved, so no confidence interval or caveat about pending announcement applies.

# 2026 401(k) Elective Deferral Limit (Pre-Catch-Up)

## 1. The answer

**$24,500.**

For tax year 2026, an employee's elective deferrals to a 401(k) plan are capped at **$24,500** under IRC §402(g)(1), before any catch-up contribution. This is the same limit that applies to 403(b) plans and to eligible 457(b) deferred compensation plans.

## 2. Authority

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| Controlling guidance | IRS Notice 2025-67, published in IRB 2025-49, page 761 (announced via IR-2025-111, "2026 cost-of-living adjustments for pension plans and retirement-related items") |
| Statutory basis | IRC §402(g)(1), as adjusted for cost-of-living under §402(g)(4) |
| Prior year | $23,500 (2025) |
| Change | +$1,000 |
| Corroborating sources | IRS "Retirement topics — 401(k) and profit-sharing plan contribution limits" ("The limit on employee elective deferrals (for traditional and safe harbor plans) is: $24,500 in 2026"); IRS COLA table, row "Elective deferrals," column 2026: 24,500 |

This is a published, finalized IRS figure — not a projection. It is the number to load into payroll and plan administration for 2026.

## 3. What the $24,500 covers

- **Pre-tax (traditional) elective deferrals** — yes, counted.
- **Designated Roth elective deferrals** — yes, counted. Pre-tax and Roth deferrals share one combined $24,500 ceiling; electing Roth does not create additional room.
- **Safe harbor 401(k) deferrals** — yes, counted; the IRS limit applies to traditional and safe harbor plans alike.
- **Deferrals across all employers** — aggregated. An employee who participates in two unrelated 401(k) plans (e.g., a full-time employer plus a solo 401(k)) has **one** $24,500 personal limit for the year, not one per plan.

## 4. What the $24,500 does NOT include

- **Employer matching contributions** — excluded from §402(g); they count against the §415(c) annual additions limit instead.
- **Employer nonelective contributions and forfeiture allocations** — excluded from §402(g); count against §415(c).
- **Catch-up contributions** — excluded from §402(g) by design. That is why the question's "before any catch-up" qualifier matters.

## 5. Neighboring 2026 limits — do not substitute these for the answer

Listed so the $24,500 is not confused with a different limit in plan communications, payroll setup, or SPD language.

| 2026 limit | Amount |
|---|---|
| **Elective deferrals, §402(g)(1) — THE ANSWER** | **$24,500** |
| Catch-up, age 50+ (§414(v)(2)(B)(i)) | $8,000 |
| Catch-up, participants attaining age 60, 61, 62, or 63 in 2026 (§414(v)(2)(E)(i)) | $11,250 |
| Maximum for an age 50–59 participant (24,500 + 8,000) | $32,500 |
| Maximum for a participant aged 60–63 in 2026 (24,500 + 11,250) | $35,750 |
| Annual additions limit, §415(c) | $72,000 |
| Compensation limit for contributions, §401(a)(17) | $360,000 |
| SIMPLE 401(k) elective deferral limit, §401(k)(11) | $17,000 |
| 457(e)(15) elective deferral limit | $24,500 |
| HCE threshold | $160,000 |

The two combined maximums ($32,500 and $35,750) are shown only to keep the catch-up figures from being mistaken for the base limit; they are outside the scope of the question, which asks for the pre-catch-up figure.

## 6. Plan-level limits that can be LOWER than $24,500

The $24,500 is a statutory ceiling, not an entitlement. An individual employee's effective 2026 limit may be lower because of:

1. **Plan document terms.** The plan may cap deferrals at a percentage of compensation or a flat dollar amount below $24,500. The IRS states plainly: "Your plan's terms may impose a lower limit on elective deferrals."
2. **Nondiscrimination testing (ADP/ACP).** Highly compensated employees may have their deferrals limited or refunded to pass the actual deferral percentage test. The IRS notes: "If you are a manager, owner, or highly compensated employee, your plan might need to limit your deferrals to pass nondiscrimination tests."
3. **§415(c) annual additions.** Where an employee receives large employer contributions in the same year, total annual additions — deferrals plus employer money — cannot exceed $72,000. This rarely binds before $24,500, but it can for employees with very large employer allocations.
4. **Compensation limits.** Deferrals are made as a percentage of pay, and only the first $360,000 of 2026 compensation counts.

## 7. HR / payroll operational guidance

**Per-pay-period withholding at the full $24,500.** Naive division creates either a shortfall or an over-deferral; use these true-up schedules so the annual total lands exactly on $24,500 and never exceeds it.

*Biweekly (26 pay periods):* $942.30 per period for periods 1–25, then $942.50 in period 26.
(942.30 × 25 = 23,557.50; 23,557.50 + 942.50 = 24,500.00)

*Semi-monthly (24 pay periods):* $1,020.83 per period for periods 1–23, then $1,020.91 in period 24.
(1,020.83 × 23 = 23,479.09; 23,479.09 + 1,020.91 = 24,500.00)

Do not use a flat $942.31 or $1,020.84 — those annualize to $24,500.06 and $24,500.16 respectively, i.e., over the limit.

**Other administrative points:**

- **Mid-year hires and comp changes** require re-amortization of the remaining periods; recalculate at each change so the year-end total is ≤ $24,500.
- **Aggregation across employers.** Because the limit is per employee and not per plan, an employee with a second job or a solo 401(k) must monitor the combined total. Payroll at one employer cannot see the other; the burden sits with the employee, and HR should say so in enrollment materials.
- **Excess deferrals.** If deferrals exceed $24,500, the excess is an "excess deferral" under §402(g)(2). It must be distributed (with allocable earnings) by April 15 of the following year to avoid double taxation; earnings are taxable in the year distributed. Plan-level correction runs through EPCRS. Flag this in the plan's correction procedure rather than netting it out informally.
- **Roth catch-up wage threshold.** §414(v)(7)(A) imposes a Roth requirement on catch-up contributions for higher-wage participants, keyed to an indexed prior-year FICA wage figure. This affects catch-up only and does not touch the $24,500 base limit; it is out of scope here and should be confirmed against the current Notice before 2026 payroll configuration.
- **Communications.** Enrollment and SPD language for 2026 should read "$24,500" for the deferral limit and separately "$8,000" (or "$11,250" for those turning 60–63 in 2026) for catch-up, so participants do not read the catch-up figure as the base.

## 8. Scope of this answer

This responds to the specific question asked: the pre-catch-up elective deferral limit for a 401(k) in tax year 2026 under U.S. federal tax law. It is written from an HR/benefits-administration standpoint and is not tax or legal advice for any individual. It assumes the question concerns a standard 401(k) (not a SIMPLE 401(k), which is $17,000 for 2026) and a participant under age 50 — the age assumption is immaterial to the answer itself, since catch-up is excluded by the terms of the question.

Should the figure ever need revisiting, the check is simple: confirm the current-year IRS cost-of-living Notice (the fall Notice in the 2025-67 series) still reports $24,500 for §402(g)(1) and that no subsequent legislation or technical correction has amended it. Absent that, $24,500 stands for 2026.
